examTips: A board question may ask you to classify numbers or decimal expansions as rational or irrational. State the reason: terminating, recurring, or non-terminating and non-recurring.
For recurring decimals, show the full working: let x equal the decimal, multiply by 10 or 100 as needed, subtract, and solve for x.
Property questions usually award marks for naming the property accurately, including the operation where needed, such as associative property over addition.
For order properties, identify whether the same number is added or multiplied and whether the multiplier is positive or negative.
When asked for rational numbers between two numbers, show the average method and make sure both answers lie strictly between the given numbers.

explain.title: Real numbers
explain.body: The real numbers are the union of rational numbers and irrational numbers: R = Q ∪ Q'. Rational numbers can be expressed as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Irrational numbers cannot be expressed as a quotient of integers.

explain.title: Decimal types
explain.body: A decimal that ends is terminating. A decimal with a repeating pattern that continues forever is non-terminating and recurring; both types are rational. A decimal that continues forever without repeating is irrational.

explain.title: Recurring decimals as fractions
explain.body: Let the recurring decimal be x. Multiply x by 10 for a one-digit repeating block, or by 100 for a two-digit repeating block. Subtract the original equation to cancel the repeating digits, then solve for x.

explain.title: Properties and inequalities
explain.body: Real-number properties describe how addition and multiplication behave. For inequalities, adding the same number to both sides keeps the inequality direction. Multiplying by a negative number reverses the direction.

explain.title: Numbers between two numbers
explain.body: One way to find a rational number between two numbers is to find their average. Repeating the method with a new pair can give another rational number between the original numbers.

mistakes: Calling every decimal that continues forever irrational: recurring decimals are rational.
Forgetting that a rational number must have a non-zero denominator.
Using 10 instead of 100 when the repeating block has two digits.
Subtracting recurring-decimal equations incorrectly so the repeating parts do not cancel.
Forgetting to reverse an inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
Naming a property without specifying whether it is over addition or multiplication when that distinction is needed.

solutions.question: Represent the following numbers on number line: √2
steps: Draw a number line and mark O as 0 and A as 1.
At A, draw a perpendicular to the number line and mark B so that AB = 1 unit.
Join O to B. By the Pythagorean theorem, OB = √(1² + 1²) = √2.
With centre O and radius OB, draw an arc to cut the number line at P.
solutions.answer: √2 is represented by the point P on the number line.
solutions.figure: A number line with 0 and 1 marked, and the point √2 marked between 1 and 2.
why: These marks set a starting point and a one-unit horizontal side.
This builds a right triangle with two sides of length 1.
The Pythagorean theorem gives the hypotenuse length as √2.
An arc transfers that length onto the number line without changing it.
The transferred length identifies the point representing √2.

At B, draw a perpendicular to OB and mark C so that BC = 1 unit.
Join O to C. By the Pythagorean theorem, OC = √((√2)² + 1²) = √3.
With centre O and radius OC, draw an arc to cut the number line at P.
solutions.answer: √3 is represented by the point P on the number line.
solutions.figure: A number line with 0, 1, 2 and 3 marked, and the point √3 marked between 1 and 2.

The first right triangle has legs of length 1, so its hypotenuse is √2.

The transferred length identifies the point representing √3.

solutions.question: Name the property used in the following: If a < b then 1/a > 1/b
steps: For non-zero a and b with ab > 0, the reciprocal property gives a < b ⇒ 1/a > 1/b.

Without this restriction, take a = −1 and b = 1: then a < b, but 1/a = −1 and 1/b = 1, so 1/a > 1/b is false.

solutions.question: Find two rational numbers between: 1/3 and 1/4
steps: The given rational numbers are 1/4 and 1/3, since 1/4 < 1/3.
A rational number between them is their mean: (1/4 + 1/3)/2 = (3/12 + 4/12)/2 = (7/12)/2 = 7/24.
why: Writing the smaller number first makes the interval’s order clear.
The mean lies halfway between two numbers, so it gives one rational number inside the interval.
Taking another mean between 7/24 and 1/3 gives a second rational number inside the interval.
The chain confirms that both numbers lie strictly between the given endpoints.

The inequalities confirm both rational numbers lie between 3 and 4.

solutions.question: Find two rational numbers between: 3/5 and 4/5

why: The mean of the endpoints lies between them and gives the first rational number.
Taking another mean gives a second number between the first mean and 4/5.
The ordered inequalities confirm both rational numbers lie between the original endpoints.

explain.body: If n is a positive integer greater than 1 and a is a real number, then any real number x such that x = ⁿ√a is called nᵗʰ root of a. Here, √ is called radical and n is the index of radical. A real number under the radical sign is called a radicand. Exponential form of x = ⁿ√a is x = (a)^(1/n).

explain.title: Laws of radicals and indices
explain.body: Use the laws to split products and quotients inside a radical, or to rewrite roots as fractional powers. For example, ⁿ√(ab) = ⁿ√a · ⁿ√b and a^m/a^n = a^(m−n). A negative exponent means take the reciprocal.

explain.title: Surds and conjugates
explain.body: An irrational radical with rational radicand is called a surd. A surd containing one term is a monomial surd; a surd containing the sum of two monomial surds is a binomial surd. √a + √b and √a − √b are called conjugate surds of each other.

explain.title: Rationalizing a denominator
explain.body: To rationalize a denominator of the form a + b√x or a − b√x, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate factor. The product of conjugate surds is a rational number.

Treating every irrational number as a surd; the radicand in a surd must be rational.

explain.title: Real numbers in everyday life
explain.body: Real numbers are used in many fields, including science and engineering, medicine and health, environmental science, computer science, navigation and transportation, surveying and architecture, and statistics. In this section, you use them to solve practical problems.

explain.title: Temperature conversions
explain.body: Use the conversion formula that matches the direction of the question: K = °C + 273; °C = 5/9 (F − 32)°; and °F = (9°C)/5 + 32. Substitute the known temperature and calculate.

explain.title: Profit and loss
explain.body: Your textbook defines: “Profit = selling Price − cost price” and “Loss = cost price − selling price”. For a percentage, compare the profit or loss with the cost price: Profit % = (profit/CP × 100) % and Loss % = (loss/CP × 100) %.

explain.title: Sharing profit and simple profit rate
explain.body: To divide a profit in a ratio, add the ratio parts and give each person their fraction of the total profit. For simple profit, your textbook gives Rate = (amount of profit × 100)/(time × principal).

explain.title: Turning words into equations
explain.body: For questions about sums, differences, or ages, assign a variable to each unknown, write an equation for each condition, and solve. Check that the result matches what the question asks for.

Rounding too early or leaving off the unit, such as °F, kelvin, or Rs.

explain.title: Rational and irrational numbers
explain.body: A rational number can be written as a ratio of integers with a non-zero denominator. A number such as √7 is irrational because 7 is not a perfect square. The real numbers include both rational and irrational numbers.

explain.title: Real-number properties
explain.body: Reflexive property means a number equals itself. Symmetric property lets us reverse an equality. Transitive property carries an equality or inequality through a middle value. Trichotomy says that for two real numbers, exactly one of <, =, or > holds.

explain.title: Distributive and associative properties
explain.body: The distributive property connects multiplication and addition, as in a(b + c) = ab + ac. The associative property changes the grouping of addition or multiplication without changing the result.

explain.title: Simplifying radicals and powers
explain.body: For a perfect-power expression under a radical, use the root index to simplify its exponents. For powers with the same base, use exponent rules and factor common powers before cancelling.

explain.title: Forming equations from problems
explain.body: Use a variable to represent an unknown quantity. Consecutive odd integers differ by 2; for a two-bucket problem, represent the larger amount using the stated difference. For simple profit at different rates, calculate each time period separately.

definitions.text:
For all real numbers a, b, c

(i) a(b + c) = ab + ac is called left distributive property of multiplication over addition.

If n is a positive integer greater than 1 and a is a real number, then any real number x such that x = ⁿ√a is called nᵗʰ root of a.
Here, √ is called radical and n is the index of radical. A real number under the radical sign is called a radicand.
Exponential form of x = ⁿ√a is x = (a)^(1/n).
An irrational radical with rational radicand is called a surd.
A surd that contains a single term is called a monomial surd e.g., √5, √7 etc.
A surd that contains the sum of two monomial surds is called a binomial surd e.g., √3 + √5, √2 + √7 etc.
√a + √b and √a − √b are called conjugate surds of each other.
The product of two conjugate surds is a rational number.
To rationalize a denominator of the form a + b√x or a − b√x, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate factor.

fullMarks: For a rational-or-irrational question, state the reason as well as the answer: terminating or recurring decimals are rational; non-terminating, non-recurring decimals are irrational.
When converting a recurring decimal to p/q, define x, multiply by 10, 100, or the needed power of 10, subtract to cancel the recurring digits, and finish by writing the fraction.
For a number-line construction, show the right triangle and its labelled lengths, use the Pythagoras step to obtain the required root, then mark and label the point on the number line.
When naming a property, give its full name carefully: distinguish commutative from associative, and identify whether a property is for equality or order.
For rationalization, multiply both numerator and denominator by the conjugate, show the denominator becoming a difference of squares, and simplify the final result.
For indices and radicals, first rewrite numbers with a common base or as fractional powers; show each index-law step before simplifying.
In a proof or verification, calculate the LHS and RHS separately, show that they are equal, and end with a clear statement that the property is verified.
mistakes: Calling a decimal irrational just because it has many digits. Fix: check whether it terminates or has a repeating pattern; only non-terminating, non-recurring decimals are irrational.
Treating every irrational number as a surd. Fix: a surd must be an irrational radical with a rational radicand; √π is not a surd.
Confusing the commutative property with the associative property. Fix: commutative changes order; associative changes grouping with brackets.
Forgetting to reverse an inequality after multiplying or dividing by a negative number. Fix: reverse < to >, or > to <, whenever the multiplier or divisor is negative.
Using the same surd instead of its conjugate when rationalizing. Fix: change the sign between the two terms, then multiply top and bottom by that conjugate.
Applying index laws to unlike bases without first rewriting them. Fix: express the terms using a common base before combining powers.
Giving only a point for a number-line question without showing the construction. Fix: draw and label the triangle or fraction divisions, mark the point, and name the value.

explain.title: Scientific notation
explain.body: A method used to express very large or very small numbers in a more manageable form is known as Scientific notation. It is commonly used in science, engineering and mathematics to simplify complex calculations.

explain.title: The required form
explain.body: A number in scientific notation is written as: a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n ∈ Z. Here “a” is called the coefficient or base number.

explain.title: Choosing the exponent's sign
explain.body: If the number is greater than 1 then n is positive and if the number is less than 1 then n is negative. When changing ordinary notation to scientific notation, moving the decimal point left gives a positive exponent; moving it right gives a negative exponent.

explain.title: Returning to ordinary notation
explain.body: If exponent is positive then the decimal will move to the right. If exponent is negative then the decimal will move to the left. Move it the number of places shown by the exponent.

explain.title: What a logarithm tells us
explain.body: In simple words, the logarithm of a real number tells us how many times one number must be multiplied by itself to get another number.

explain.title: Parts of a logarithm
explain.body: The general form of a logarithm is: log_b x = y. Where: b is the base, x is the result or the number whose logarithm is being taken, and y is the exponent or the logarithm of x to the base b.

explain.title: The key conversion
explain.body: log_b x = y  ⇔  bʸ = x where b > 0, x > 0 and b ≠ 1. In words, "the logarithm of x to the base b is y," means that when b is raised to the power y, it equals x.

explain.title: Finding an unknown
explain.body: Change the logarithmic equation into exponential form. Then solve the power equation for the unknown.

mistakes: Mixing up the base, result, and exponent when changing forms.

Dropping a negative sign in an exponent or logarithm value.
Confusing the result x with the exponent y in log_b x = y.
Giving an answer without showing the exponential form when the question asks you to find an unknown.

explain.title: Common logarithm
explain.body: The **common logarithm** is the logarithm with a base of 10. It is written as log_10 or simply as log (when no base is mentioned, it is usually assumed to be base 10). For example, 10² = 100, so log 100 = 2.

explain.title: Characteristic
explain.body: The characteristic is the integral part of the logarithm. It tells us how big or small the number is. For a number greater than 1, subtract 1 from its digits to the left of the decimal point. For a number less than 1, use the negative of (the number of zeros before the first non-zero digit + 1). When the characteristic is negative, we write it with bar.

explain.title: Mantissa
explain.body: The mantissa is the decimal part of the logarithm. It represents the "fractional" component and is always positive. For example, in log 5000 = 3.698 the mantissa is 0.698.

explain.title: Using the logarithm table
explain.body: Find the characteristic from the size of the number. Use the first digits to find the table entry, and use the next digit for the column; add a mean difference when the table method requires it. Then combine characteristic and mantissa.

explain.title: Antilogarithm and natural logarithm
explain.body: An antilogarithm is the inverse operation of a logarithm. It helps to find a number whose logarithmic value is given. The natural logarithm is the logarithm with base e, where e is approximately equal to 2.71828; it is denoted as ln.

explain.title: Product Law
explain.body: log_b xy = log_b x + log_b y. The logarithm of the product is the sum of the logarithms of the factors.

explain.title: Quotient Law
explain.body: log_b (x/y) = log_b x − log_b y. The logarithm of a quotient is the difference between the logarithms of the numerator and the denominator.

explain.title: Power Law
explain.body: log_b xⁿ = n × log_b x. The logarithm of a number raised to a power is the product of the power and the logarithm of the base number.

explain.title: Change of Base Law
explain.body: log_b x = (log_a x)/(log_a b). This law allows to change the base of a logarithm from “b” to any other base “a”.

explain.title: Scientific notation
explain.body: Write a number as a coefficient times a power of 10. The coefficient should be at least 1 and less than 10. Moving the decimal left gives a positive exponent; moving it right gives a negative exponent.

explain.title: Logarithmic and exponential forms
explain.body: The forms aᵇ = c and logₐ c = b say the same thing: a raised to b gives c. The base stays the base, the result becomes the logarithm's argument, and the exponent becomes its value.

explain.title: Common logarithms
explain.body: A common logarithm has base 10, usually written without showing the base. For example, log 100 = 2 because 10² = 100. The logarithm of zero is undefined.

explain.title: Laws of logarithms
explain.body: Use log A + log B = log (AB), log A − log B = log (A/B), and k log A = log Aᵏ. These laws help you combine or expand logarithmic expressions.

explain.title: Solving logarithmic equations
explain.body: Rewrite a logarithmic equation in exponential form. For exponential equations with the same base on both sides, equate the exponents and solve.

explain.title: Applications and numerical work
explain.body: For growth models, substitute the target value, solve for the time, and interpret the time in context. For calculations with logarithm tables, combine logarithms and then find the antilogarithm.

mistakes: In scientific notation, moving the decimal to the right requires a negative power of 10; moving it to the left requires a positive power.
When converting forms, do not swap the base and the argument: aᵇ = c becomes logₐ c = b.
Use addition of logarithms for multiplication and subtraction of logarithms for division; do not reverse these laws.
When using the power law, multiply the exponent too: 3 log y² = log y⁶, not log y³.
log 0 is undefined, not zero.
In a growth-model answer, distinguish t years after 2016 from the calendar year: add t to 2016.

solutions.question: In the year 2016, the population of a city was 22 millions and was growing at a rate of 2.5% per year. The function p(t) = 22(1.025)ᵗ gives the population in millions, t years after 2016. Use the model to determine in which year the population will reach 35 millions. steps: Taking logarithms, t log 1.025 = log 35 − log 22.
To the nearest year, t ≈ 19 years.

Dividing both sides by 22 isolates the exponential part.
The logarithm power and quotient laws bring down t and express the ratio as a difference.
Dividing by log 1.025 isolates the number of years t.
Substituting the table values gives the approximate time after 2016.

definitions.text: A method used to express very large or very small numbers in a more manageable form is known as Scientific notation. It is commonly used in science, engineering and mathematics to simplify complex calculations.

A number in scientific notation is written as:
a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n ∈ Z
Here “a” is called the coefficient or base number.

definitions.term: Rule for the sign of the exponent in scientific notation
definitions.text: If the number is greater than 1 then n is positive and if the number is less than 1 then n is negative.

definitions.term: Rule for converting scientific notation to ordinary notation
definitions.text:
If exponent is positive then the decimal will move to the right.
If exponent is negative then the decimal will move to the left.

The relationship between logarithmic form and exponential form is given below:

log_b x = y  ⇔  bʸ = x where b > 0, x > 0 and b ≠ 1
The common logarithm is the logarithm with a base of 10. It is written as log_10 or simply as log (when no base is mentioned, it is usually assumed to be base 10).
The characteristic is the integral part of the logarithm. It tells us how big or small the number is.

definitions.term: Rule for finding the characteristic of a number greater than 1
definitions.text: Characteristic = number of digits to the left of the decimal point − 1

definitions.term: Rule for finding the characteristic of a number less than 1
definitions.text: Characteristic = − (number of zeros between the decimal point and the first non-zero digit + 1)

definitions.term: Rule for writing a negative characteristic
definitions.text: When the characteristic is negative, we write it with bar.
The mantissa is the decimal part of the logarithm. It represents the "fractional" component and is always positive.
log (Number) = Characteristic + Mantissa
An antilogarithm is the inverse operation of a logarithm. An antilogarithm helps to find a number whose logarithmic value is given.
If log_b x = y ⇔ b^y = x then the process of finding x is called antilogarithm of y.
The natural logarithm is the logarithm with base e, where e is a mathematical constant approximately equal to 2.71828. It is denoted as ln.
The logarithm of the product is the sum of the logarithms of the factors.
The logarithm of a quotient is the difference between the logarithms of the numerator and the denominator.
The logarithm of a number raised to a power is the product of the power and the logarithm of the base number.
This law allows to change the base of a logarithm from “b” to any other base “a”.

fullMarks: For scientific notation, first move the decimal until the coefficient is at least 1 but less than 10; then count the places and write the power of 10.
Check the exponent sign: moving the decimal left to make scientific notation gives a positive exponent for numbers greater than 1; numbers less than 1 have a negative exponent.
For ordinary notation, show the decimal-point movement and place enough zeros so the decimal moves exactly the number of places shown by the exponent.
When changing forms of a logarithm, identify the base, result and exponent correctly: log_b x = y means bʸ = x.
For characteristic questions, show the digit or zero count. Write a negative characteristic with a bar, such as 2̅, so it is not confused with a negative mantissa.
For logarithm-table questions, show the characteristic, table row and column, mean difference if needed, and the final combined logarithm.
For finding x from log x, show how you make a negative mantissa positive, state the characteristic and mantissa, then show the antilog and decimal-point placement.
For scientific-notation answers involving a measured quantity, retain the unit given in the question, such as metres per second or km.
mistakes: Using a positive exponent for a number smaller than 1 in scientific notation. Fix: move the decimal to make the coefficient between 1 and 10, then use a negative exponent.
Writing a coefficient of 10 or more in scientific notation. Fix: adjust the decimal until 1 ≤ a < 10 and update the exponent.
Moving the decimal in the wrong direction when converting to ordinary notation. Fix: a positive exponent moves it right; a negative exponent moves it left.
Mixing up the base, result and exponent when converting logarithmic and exponential forms. Fix: in log_b x = y, write bʸ = x.
Counting the decimal point itself as a zero when finding a characteristic below 1. Fix: count only the zeros between the decimal point and the first non-zero digit, then add 1.
Writing a negative characteristic as an ordinary negative decimal and making the mantissa negative too. Fix: use bar notation for the characteristic and keep the mantissa positive.
Placing the decimal point incorrectly in an antilogarithm answer. Fix: use the characteristic to place the decimal relative to the first non-zero digit in the table value.

explain.title: Patterns
explain.body: A mathematical pattern is a predictable arrangement of numbers, shapes, or symbols that follows a specific rule or relationship. For example, in 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, each term is found by adding 3 to the previous term.

explain.title: Structures and relationships
explain.body: A mathematical structure is a collection of items or objects, along with particular relationships defined among them. Looking for how parts repeat or connect helps us understand the structure. We can also establish a relationship between two sets when there is a correspondence between the numbers of these sets.

explain.title: Sets and their forms
explain.body: A set is described as a well-defined collection of distinct objects, numbers or elements, so that we may be able to decide whether the object belongs to the collection or not. A set can be described in words, by listing its elements in tabular (roster) form, or by stating a shared property in set-builder form.

explain.title: Membership and subsets
explain.body: The symbol ∈ means that an element belongs to a set, and ∉ means it does not belong. If every element of A is an element of B, then A is a subset of B. A proper subset is not equal to the larger set.

explain.title: Empty set and power set
explain.body: The empty set has no elements, while a singleton set has one element. The power set of a set S denoted by P(S) is the set containing all the possible subsets of S. If S has m elements, its power set has 2^m elements.

mistakes: Do not confuse {0}, which has one element, with ∅, which has no elements.
Do not confuse equal sets, which have the same elements, with equivalent sets, which have the same number of elements.
Do not forget that a power set includes the empty set and the original set.
Count an element that is itself a set as one element; for example, {a, {b, c}} has two elements.
In set-builder notation, include the correct number set and the correct bounds.
Remember that a proper subset cannot be equal to the original set.

solutions.question: Write the following sets in set builder notation: {1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, …, 484}
steps: The given numbers are squares of natural numbers: 1=1², 4=2², 9=3², …, 484=22².
why: Recognizing each entry as a square reveals the pattern and its final index.
This describes the set using square numbers with indices from 1 through 22.

solutions.question: Write the following sets in set builder notation: {2, 4, 8, 16, …, 256}
steps: The given numbers are powers of 2: 2=2¹, 4=2², 8=2³, …, 256=2⁸.
why: Recognizing each entry as a power of 2 reveals the pattern and its final exponent.
This describes the set using powers with exponents from 1 through 8.

solutions.question: Write the following sets in set builder notation: {0, ±1, ±2, …, ±1000}
steps: The given set contains all integers from −1000 to 1000, inclusive.
why: The entries are precisely the integers within the stated inclusive bounds.
This set-builder condition includes every integer from −1000 to 1000.

solutions.question: Write the following sets in set builder notation: {6, 12, 18, …, 120}
steps: The given numbers are multiples of 6: 6=6×1, 12=6×2, 18=6×3, …, 120=6×20.
why: The constant difference of 6 shows each term is six times a counting number.
The bounds on n select exactly the listed multiples, from 6 through 120.

solutions.question: Write the following sets in set builder notation: {100, 102, 104, …, 400}
steps: The first number is 100 and each successive number increases by 2.
Write the terms as x=100+2n, where n∈W.
For the first term, 100=100+2(0), so n=0.
For the last term, 400=100+2n; hence 2n=300 and n=150.
why: A constant increase of 2 shows the terms follow an arithmetic pattern.
This rule generates even numbers starting at 100 when n begins at zero.
Substituting the first term finds the starting value of n.
Solving with the last term finds the ending value of n.
These bounds include every index from the first term to the last.

solutions.question: Write the following sets in set builder notation: {1, 3, 9, 27, 81, …}
steps: The given numbers are powers of 3: 1=3⁰, 3=3¹, 9=3², 27=3³, ….
why: Each term is a power of 3, including 1 because 3⁰ equals 1.
Whole-number exponents generate the listed powers and continue the pattern.

solutions.question: Write the following sets in set builder notation: {1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50, 100}
steps: Each element of the given set divides 100 exactly.
Thus, x is a divisor of 100.
why: A divisor is a number that divides another number without a remainder.
This condition describes exactly the elements of the given set.

solutions.question: Write the following sets in set builder notation: {5, 10, 15, …, 100}
steps: The given numbers are multiples of 5: 5=5×1, 10=5×2, 15=5×3, …, 100=5×20.
why: A constant factor of 5 identifies the terms as multiples of 5.
The bounds on n include all listed multiples, from 5 through 100.

solutions.question: Write the following sets in set builder notation: The set of all integers between −100 and 1000
steps: An integer between −100 and 1000 is an integer x such that −100 < x < 1000.
Using set builder notation, the set is {x | x ∈ Z ∧ −100 < x < 1000}.
why: The phrase “between” gives strict bounds, while the set must contain integers.
This notation combines integer membership with both strict bounds.

solutions.question: Write each of the following sets in tabular forms: {x | x is a multiple of 3 ∧ x ≤ 36}
steps: The positive multiples of 3 not greater than 36 are 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33 and 36.
Writing these elements in tabular form gives {3, 6, 9, …, 36}.
why: Listing the positive multiples shows every qualifying value up to 36.

solutions.question: Write each of the following sets in tabular forms: {x | x ∈ N ∧ x + 4 = 0}
steps: For x ∈ N, x + 4 = 0 gives x = −4.
Since −4 ∉ N, there is no element in the set.
In tabular form, the set is {}.
why: Subtracting 4 from both sides solves the equation for x.
Natural numbers cannot be negative, so this value cannot belong.
An empty pair of braces represents a set with no elements.

solutions.question: Write each of the following sets in tabular forms: {x | x ∈ N ∧ x = x}
steps: The condition x = x is true for every natural number x.
Therefore the set contains all natural numbers.
In tabular form, the set is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, …}.
why: The identity rule says every number equals itself, so the condition excludes no natural numbers.
A set-builder condition includes every natural number that satisfies its condition.
Listing the natural numbers with dots shows the pattern continues without end.

solutions.question: Write each of the following sets in tabular forms: {x | x ∈ Z ∧ 3x + 1 = 0}
why: Start with the given equation so we can solve for its possible value of x.
Subtracting 1 from both sides keeps the equation balanced and isolates the term with x.
Dividing both sides by 3 isolates x.
Integers have no fractional values, so this solution is not an integer.
Since no integer satisfies the condition, the set is empty.

solutions.question: Write two proper subsets of each of the following sets: {a, b, c}
why: A proper subset contains only elements from the larger set and is not equal to it.
The same subset rule shows that b belongs to the larger set, while the sets are unequal.

solutions.question: Write two proper subsets of each of the following sets: {0, 1}
why: The element 0 belongs to the original set, and the singleton is smaller than it.
The element 1 belongs to the original set, and the singleton is smaller than it.

solutions.question: Write two proper subsets of each of the following sets: N
why: The empty set is a subset of every set, and it differs from the natural numbers.
Since 1 is natural, its singleton is a subset and is smaller than N.

solutions.question: Write two proper subsets of each of the following sets: Z
why: Zero is an integer, so its singleton is a subset and is smaller than Z.
One is an integer, so its singleton is a subset and is smaller than Z.

solutions.question: Write two proper subsets of each of the following sets: Q
why: Zero is rational, so its singleton is a subset and is smaller than Q.
One-half is a ratio of integers, so its singleton is a proper subset of Q.

solutions.question: Write two proper subsets of each of the following sets: R
why: Zero is real, so its singleton is a subset and is smaller than R.
One is real, so its singleton is a subset and is smaller than R.

solutions.question: Write two proper subsets of each of the following sets: {x | x ∈ Q ∧ 0 < x ≤ 2}
steps: Choose A = {1/2, 1, 3/2}; each element of A is rational and satisfies 0 < x ≤ 2, so A ⊆ S.
Since 2 ∈ S but 2 ∉ A, A is a proper subset of S.
Choose B = {1, 2}; each element of B is rational and satisfies 0 < x ≤ 2, so B ⊆ S.
Since 1/2 ∈ S but 1/2 ∉ B, B is a proper subset of S.

solutions.question: Is there any set which has no proper subset? If so, name that set.
steps: The empty set has only one subset, namely the empty set itself.
A proper subset must be different from the set.
Therefore, the empty set has no proper subset.
why: The empty set contains no elements, so its only possible subset is itself.
By definition, a proper subset must not equal the original set.
Thus its only subset fails the definition of a proper subset.

solutions.question: What is the difference between {a, b} and {{a, b}}?
steps: The set {a, b} has two elements, a and b.
The set {{a, b}} has one element, namely the set {a, b}.
solutions.answer: {a, b} contains two elements, a and b, while {{a, b}} contains one element, {a, b}.
solutions.bookAnswer: {a, b} is a set containing two elements a and b while {{a, b}} is a set containing one element {a, b}
why: A comma separates elements, so a and b count as two separate elements.
The outer braces contain one element: the entire set written inside them.

solutions.question: What is the number of elements of the power set of each of the following sets? { }
steps: The number of elements of A is n = 0.
The number of elements of the power set of A is 2ⁿ = 2⁰ = 1.
why: Naming the given set A makes it easier to count its elements.
The empty set has no elements, so its cardinality is zero.
A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, so here the power set has one element.

solutions.question: What is the number of elements of the power set of each of the following sets? {0, 1}
steps: The number of elements of A is n = 2.
The number of elements of the power set of A is 2ⁿ = 2² = 4.
why: Naming the set makes it easier to apply the power-set rule.
Counting the distinct elements gives the value of n.
Each element can be included or excluded, so a set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets.

solutions.question: What is the number of elements of the power set of each of the following sets? {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}
steps: The number of elements of A is n = 7.
The number of elements of the power set of A is 2ⁿ = 2⁷ = 128.
why: Naming the set makes it easier to apply the power-set rule.
Counting the distinct elements gives the value of n.
Each element can be included or excluded, so a set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets.

solutions.question: What is the number of elements of the power set of each of the following sets? {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}
steps: The number of elements of A is n = 8.
The number of elements of the power set of A is 2ⁿ = 2⁸ = 256.
why: Naming the set makes it easier to apply the power-set rule.
Counting the distinct elements gives the value of n.
Each element can be included or excluded, so a set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets.

solutions.question: What is the number of elements of the power set of each of the following sets? {a, {b, c}}
steps: The number of elements of A is n = 2.
The number of elements of the power set of A is 2ⁿ = 2² = 4.
why: Naming the set helps us count its elements clearly.
The set has two elements because a and {b, c} each count as one element.
A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, since each element is included or excluded.

solutions.question: What is the number of elements of the power set of each of the following sets? {{a, b}, {b, c}, {d, e}}
steps: The number of elements of A is n = 3.
The number of elements of the power set of A is 2ⁿ = 2³ = 8.
why: Naming the set helps us count its elements clearly.
The three listed sets are the three distinct elements of A.
A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, since each element is included or excluded.

solutions.question: Write down the power set of each of the following sets: {9, 11}
steps: The power set contains all subsets of {9, 11}.
The subset with no elements is ∅.
The subsets with one element are {9} and {11}.
The subset with two elements is {9, 11}.
why: A power set is defined as the collection of every subset.
Every set has the empty set as a subset.
Choosing either single element gives all subsets containing exactly one element.
Taking both elements gives the only subset containing exactly two elements.
This collects all four subsets into the power set.

solutions.question: Write down the power set of each of the following sets: {+, −, ×, ÷}
steps: The power set contains all subsets of {+, −, ×, ÷}.
The subset with no elements is ∅.
The subsets with one element are {+}, {−}, {×}, {÷}.
The subsets with two elements are {+, −}, {+, ×}, {+, ÷}, {−, ×}, {−, ÷}, {×, ÷}.
The subsets with three elements are {+, −, ×}, {+, −, ÷}, {+, ×, ÷}, {−, ×, ÷}.
The subset with four elements is {+, −, ×, ÷}.
why: A power set is defined as the collection of every subset.
The empty set is a subset of every set.
Each listed subset is made by choosing one of the four elements.
Choosing each possible pair lists all subsets with two elements.
Choosing three of the four elements lists every three-element subset.
Using all four elements gives the only four-element subset.
This combines the empty subset and all non-empty subsets.

solutions.question: Write down the power set of each of the following sets: {∅}
steps: The set {∅} has one element, namely ∅.
Its subsets are the empty set ∅ and the set containing its element, {∅}.
why: The notation shows that the empty set itself is the single element of this set.
A one-element set has exactly two subsets: the empty set and the whole set.
These are both subsets, so together they form the power set.

solutions.question: Write down the power set of each of the following sets: {a, {b, c}}
steps: The set {a, {b, c}} has two elements: a and {b, c}.
The subset with no elements is ∅.
The subsets with one element are {a} and {{b, c}}.
The subset with two elements is {a, {b, c}}.
why: The inner set {b, c} counts as one element of the outer set.
The empty set is always a subset.
Selecting each outer element separately gives the one-element subsets.
Selecting both outer elements gives the whole set as a subset.
This lists every subset and therefore gives the power set.

examTips: Board questions commonly ask you to find a union, intersection, difference or complement from sets or a Venn diagram.
For two-set counting questions, write n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) before substituting values; this earns method marks.
For three-set questions, show the full inclusion-exclusion formula, including the plus sign before the triple intersection, then substitute and simplify.
For questions asking for people who like none, subtract the union count from the universal-set count.
For a Venn diagram question, fill the centre first, then the pairwise-only regions, then the single-set-only regions; show all given information and labels.

explain.title: Union and intersection
explain.body: The union A ∪ B contains elements in A or B, including elements in both. The intersection A ∩ B contains only elements that belong to both sets. Your textbook defines the union as “The union of two sets A and B, denoted by A∪B, is the set of all elements which belong to A or B.” It defines the intersection as “The intersection of two sets A and B, denoted by A ∩ B, is the set of all elements that belong to both A and B.”

explain.title: Difference and complement
explain.body: A − B keeps elements in A but not in B, so in general A − B ≠ B − A. The complement A′ contains elements of the universal set U that are not in A. Your textbook defines the difference as “The difference between the sets A and B denoted by A−B, consists of all the elements that belong to A but do not belong to B.” It defines the complement as “The complement of a set A, denoted by A' or A^c relative to the universal set U is the set of all elements of U, which do not belong to A.”

explain.title: Disjoint and overlapping sets
explain.body: Your textbook defines disjoint sets this way: “If the intersection of two sets is the empty set, the sets are said to be disjoint.” It defines overlapping sets this way: “If the intersection of two sets is non-empty but neither is a subset of the other, the sets are called overlapping sets.”

explain.title: Counting elements
explain.body: Your textbook defines cardinality as “The cardinality of a set is defined as the total number of elements of a set.” For two sets, n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). For three sets, subtract the pairwise intersections and then add the triple intersection.

explain.title: De Morgan’s Laws
explain.body: The complement of a union is the intersection of the complements: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′. The complement of an intersection is the union of the complements: (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.

mistakes: Do not confuse ∪ (or) with ∩ (and).
Do not count a shared element twice when finding a union; subtract the intersection.
Do not assume A − B equals B − A; set difference is not commutative.
When finding a complement, use the stated universal set U; elements outside U cannot be included.
For three sets, subtract all three pairwise intersections and add the triple intersection once.
In a Venn diagram, pairwise intersection counts may include the central triple intersection unless the question explicitly says “only.”

explain.title: Relations and ordered pairs
explain.body: Mathematically, a relation is any set of ordered pairs. The first elements make the domain; the second elements make the range. For example, if r = {(1, 4), (2, 3)}, then Dom r = {1, 2} and Ran r = {4, 3}.

explain.title: What makes a relation a function?
explain.body: A function is a relation from A to B whose domain is A and whose ordered pairs do not have equal first elements. In other words, each input has one output. Different inputs may still have the same output.

explain.title: Types of functions
explain.body: An into function has Range f ⊂ B and Range f ≠ B. An onto function has Range f = B. A bijective function is both one-one and onto.

explain.title: Finding function values and constants
explain.body: To find f(k), replace every x in the function rule with k. If a rule contains unknown constants, substitute the given function values to form equations, then solve them together.

explain.title: Linear and quadratic functions
explain.body: The function {(x, y) | y = mx + c} is called a linear function because its graph is a straight line. The function {(x, y) | y = ax² + bx + c} is called a quadratic function.

explain.title: Set notation and listing
explain.body: A set-builder description tells you which elements belong in a set. To write a set in tabular form, list its members inside braces. Check the number system and any restrictions in the description.

explain.title: Set operations
explain.body: A ∪ B contains elements in A or B or both. A ∩ B contains elements common to both. A − B contains elements in A but not in B. A′ contains elements in the universal set U that are not in A.

explain.title: Counting unions
explain.body: For two sets, n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). Subtract the intersection because it was counted once in each set.

explain.title: Three-set counting
explain.body: For three sets, add the three individual counts, subtract the three pairwise intersections, then add the triple intersection. This corrects the repeated counting.

explain.title: Cartesian products and functions
explain.body: The number of ordered pairs in A × B is n(A) × n(B). To evaluate a function, replace x with the input value and simplify using the correct order of operations.

mistakes: Counting shared elements twice when finding a union.
Forgetting that a complement is taken relative to the universal set U.
Confusing A − B with B − A; set difference is not generally reversible.
For a Cartesian product, adding the set sizes instead of multiplying them.
Substituting a function input incorrectly, especially when the input is negative or a fraction.
In three-set inclusion-exclusion, forgetting to add the triple intersection back.

definitions.text: A mathematical pattern is a predictable arrangement of numbers, shapes, or symbols that follows a specific rule or relationship.
A mathematical structure is typically a rule of a numerical, geometric and logical relationship that holds consistency within a specific domain.
A set is described as a well-defined collection of distinct objects, numbers or elements, so that we may be able to decide whether the object belongs to the collection or not.
A set may be described in words.
A set may be described by listing its elements within brackets.

It is sometimes more convenient or useful to employ the method of set-builder notation in specifying sets. This is done by using a symbol or letter for an arbitrary set member and stating the property common to all the members.
N = The set of natural numbers = {1, 2, 3, …}
W = The set of whole numbers = {0, 1, 2, …}
Z = The set of integers = {0, ±1, ±2, …}
O = The set of odd integers = {±1, ±3, ±5, …}
E = The set of even integers = {0, ±2, ±4, …}
P = The set of prime numbers = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, …}
Q = The set of all rational numbers = {x | x = p/q where p, q ∈ Z and q ≠ 0}
Q′ = The set of all irrational numbers = {x | x ≠ p/q, where p, q ∈ Z and q ≠ 0}
R = The set of all real numbers = Q ∪ Q′
A set with only one element is called a singleton set.
The set with no elements (zero number of elements) is called an empty set, null set, or Void set.
Two sets A and B are equal if they have exactly the same elements or if every element of set A is an element of set B.
Two sets A and B are equivalent if they have the same number of elements.
If every element of a set A is an element of set B, then A is a subset of B.
If A is a subset of B and B contains at least one element that is not an element of A, then A is said to be a proper subset of B.
If A is a subset of B and A = B, then we say that A is an improper subset of B.
The set that contains all objects or elements under consideration is called the universal set or the universe of discourse.
The power set of a set S denoted by P(S) is the set containing all the possible subsets of S.
The union of two sets A and B, denoted by A∪B, is the set of all elements which belong to A or B.
The intersection of two sets A and B, denoted by A ∩ B, is the set of all elements that belong to both A and B.
If the intersection of two sets is the empty set, the sets are said to be disjoint.
If the intersection of two sets is non-empty but neither is a subset of the other, the sets are called overlapping sets
The difference between the sets A and B denoted by A−B, consists of all the elements that belong to A but do not belong to B.
The complement of a set A, denoted by A' or A^c relative to the universal set U is the set of all elements of U, which do not belong to A.
The cardinality of a set is defined as the total number of elements of a set.

definitions.term: Principle of inclusion and exclusion for two sets
definitions.text:
Let A and B be finite sets, then
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
and A ∪ B and A ∩ B are also finite.

definitions.term: Principle of inclusion and exclusion for three sets
definitions.text:
If A, B and C are finite sets, then
n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) − n(B ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C)
and A ∪ B ∪ C, A ∩ B, A ∩ C, B ∩ C and A ∩ B ∩ C are also finite.

formulas.formula: A ⊆ B iff ∀ x ∈ A ⇒ x ∈ B
formulas.use: Use to show that A is a subset of B.
Use to find the number of subsets of a finite set.

formulas.formula: A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A ∨ x ∈ B}
formulas.use: Use to list elements in A, in B, or in both.

formulas.formula: A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A ∧ x ∈ B}
formulas.use: Use to list elements common to both sets.

formulas.formula: A − B = {x | x ∈ A ∧ x ∉ B}
formulas.use: Use to find elements in A but not in B.

formulas.formula: A' = {x | x ∈ U ∧ x ∉ A} = U − A
formulas.use: Use to find the complement of A in the stated universal set U.

formulas.formula: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
formulas.use: Use for the total in either of two finite sets.

formulas.formula: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) − n(B ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C)
formulas.use: Use for the total in at least one of three finite sets.

formulas.formula: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B), when A ∩ B = ∅
formulas.use: Use when the two sets are disjoint.
Use to count the elements in A but not in B.
Commutative property of union.
Commutative property of intersection.
Associative property of union.
Associative property of intersection.
Distributivity of union over intersection.
Distributivity of intersection over union.
First of De Morgan’s Laws.
Second of De Morgan’s Laws.

formulas.formula: A ∪ B = B when A ⊆ B; A ∩ B = A when A ⊆ B
formulas.use: Use when one set is contained in the other.

fullMarks: For a set-builder answer, state both the type of elements and every needed condition or bound; do not leave the set unlimited when the question gives an endpoint.
For tabular form, list each distinct element once inside braces. Use ∅ for no elements; do not confuse ∅ with {0}.
For power-set questions, count the elements of the original set first. Treat a set written as an element, such as {b, c}, as one element when counting.
For complements, write or identify the universal set U first, then list only the elements of U that are not in the given set.
For a Venn-diagram answer, draw and label the rectangle U and every circle. Fill the shared regions first, then the exclusive regions, and show elements outside the circles if required.
For verification questions, calculate both sides separately, show the resulting sets, and finish with the equality statement.
For word problems, define the sets and write the known cardinalities before applying inclusion-exclusion. Show the substitution and arithmetic, then finish with a sentence answering the question.
Cardinality answers count elements or people, not set notation; include the appropriate unit or context in the final sentence.
mistakes: Writing {0} for the empty set. Fix: {0} contains one element; use ∅ or {} when there are no elements.
Treating repeated elements as extra elements in a set or in its cardinality. Fix: list each distinct element only once.
Counting {b, c} as two elements in {a, {b, c}}. Fix: the inner set {b, c} is one element of the outer set.
Finding a complement without using the stated universal set. Fix: write U first and subtract the given set from U.
Reversing a set difference, or assuming A − B = B − A. Fix: A − B keeps elements in A that are not in B; order matters.
In inclusion-exclusion for three sets, subtracting pairwise overlaps but forgetting to add the triple overlap back. Fix: use the full formula and check that the final triple term is added.

In a Venn diagram, putting pairwise intersection totals directly into the pair-only regions when they include the triple intersection. Fix: subtract the triple intersection from each pair total before filling pair-only regions.

explain.title: Common factors
explain.body: In algebra, a common factor is an expression that divides two or more expressions exactly. For example, 2x − 6 = 2(x − 3), so 2 is a common factor of both terms.

explain.title: Trinomials and binomials
explain.body: Trinomial factoring is converting trinomial expression as a product of two binomial expressions. A trinomial is an expression with three terms and binomial is an expression with two terms.

explain.title: Factor quadratics by grouping
explain.body: For x² + px + q, find two numbers whose product is q and whose sum is p. For ax² + bx + c, multiply a by c, find a factor pair with the required sum, split the middle term, and group.

explain.title: Use identities for quartics and cubes
explain.body: A quartic expression may be rewritten as a difference of squares. For cubes, use a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) or a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).

mistakes: Taking out a factor that is not common to every term, or not taking out the highest common factor.

Assuming (a + b)² = a² + b² or (a + b)³ = a³ + b³.

explain.title: Highest Common Factor
explain.body: The HCF of two or more algebraic expressions refers to the greatest algebraic expression which divides them without leaving a remainder. Factor each expression, then multiply only the factors shared by all of them.

explain.title: HCF by division
explain.body: Divide the polynomial with the higher degree by the other polynomial. If there is a remainder, continue using the divisor and remainder. A constant factor that is not common to all the given polynomials is ignored, as shown in your textbook.

explain.title: Least Common Multiple
explain.body: The LCM of two or more algebraic expressions is the smallest expression that is divisible by each of the given expressions. By factorization, use the factors required by the expressions, taking each factor at its greatest required power.

explain.title: Relationship between LCM and HCF
explain.body: For two polynomials, LCM × HCF = p(x) × q(x). To find a missing polynomial, divide LCM × HCF by the polynomial already given. To find the product, multiply the LCM by the HCF.

mistakes: For the HCF, including a factor that is not common to every expression.

Forgetting to factor completely before identifying common or required factors.

Leaving out the zero remainder when showing division proves that one polynomial divides another.

explain.title: What a square root means
explain.body: The square root of an algebraic expression refers to a value that, when multiplied by itself, gives the original expression. Just like finding the square root of a number, taking the square root of an algebraic expression involves determining what expression, when squared, results in the given expression.

explain.title: Factorization method
explain.body: Rewrite the polynomial as a perfect square, such as (x − 4)². Then take the square root of the square factor and follow your textbook's sign notation.

explain.title: Division method
explain.body: When the degree of the polynomial is higher, division method in finding the square root is very useful. Start with the square root of the leading term, double the root found so far to obtain the next term, and continue until the remainder is zero.

explain.title: Using factors in applications
explain.body: For a question asking when a function is zero, factorize the expression and set each variable factor equal to zero. Then state the values of x.

fullMarks: For a common-factor question, take out the greatest factor shared by every term first; check that dividing each term by it leaves the correct bracket.
For a trinomial, show the two numbers you chose and check their product and sum before splitting the middle term.
For ax² + bx + c, show the product ac, split bx into two terms, then factor by grouping. Do not skip straight to the answer.
For quartic and four-binomial products, show the useful pairing or substitution, factor the simpler expression, and substitute back into the original variable.
For HCF and LCM questions, factorize every expression completely. Use only common factors for the HCF; for the LCM include each factor to the greatest power needed.
For a division-method HCF question, write the polynomial division steps clearly and state the last non-zero remainder as the HCF.
For questions using LCM × HCF = product, write the relationship first, substitute the given expressions, and simplify before stating the answer.
Keep signs and powers clear in every factor, and finish with a labelled final statement such as “Hence, HCF = …” or “Hence, the factorization is …”.
mistakes: Choosing two numbers for a monic trinomial that add to the constant instead of multiplying to it. Fix: check that their product is q and their sum is p.
For ax² + bx + c, splitting the middle term using numbers whose sum is b but whose product is not ac. Fix: check both conditions before grouping.
For a sum of cubes, using the difference-of-cubes signs in the second factor. Fix: a³ + b³ has a + b first and a² − ab + b² second.
For a difference of cubes, writing a² − ab + b² as the second factor. Fix: a³ − b³ uses a − b and then a² + ab + b².
Finding an HCF by including factors that are not shared by every expression. Fix: keep only the common factors, using the smallest power shared.
Finding an LCM by using only the common factors. Fix: include all factors needed to make the LCM divisible by every given expression, using the greatest power required.
Stopping after substituting y or another temporary expression. Fix: replace the substitution with the original expression in the final factorized answer.

explain.body: An equation of the form ax + b = 0 where ‘a’ and ‘b’ are constants, a ≠ 0 and ‘x’ is a variable, is called a linear equation in one variable. In linear equation, the highest power of the variable is always 1.

explain.title: Inequality symbols
explain.body: The four symbols are > (greater than), < (less than), ≥ (greater than or equal to), and ≤ (less than or equal to). Adding or subtracting the same constant on each side, or multiplying or dividing each side by a positive constant, does not change the order. Multiplying or dividing by a negative constant changes the order.

explain.title: One-variable solutions
explain.body: Solve an inequality as you would an equation, but reverse its order if you multiply or divide by a negative constant. A strict inequality has an open endpoint on a real line; an inequality with ≥ or ≤ has a filled endpoint.

explain.title: Half-planes and boundary lines
explain.body: The graph of the corresponding equation is the boundary line. It divides the plane into two half-planes. Use a dashed line for > or < because the boundary is not included, and a solid line for ≥ or ≤ because it is included.

explain.title: Testing a point and graphing a system
explain.body: Choose a point not on the boundary line, usually (0, 0), and substitute its coordinates into the inequality. If it makes the inequality true, shade the side containing that point; otherwise shade the opposite side. For a system, the common shaded region is the solution region.

yourTurn.question: Maximize f(x, y) = 2x + 5y; subject to the constraints 2y − x ≤ 8 ; x − y ≤ 4 ; x ≥ 0; y ≥ 0
solution: The associated equations are 2y − x = 8 and x − y = 4.
For x − y = 4, the intercepts are (4, 0) and (0, −4); for 2y − x = 8, the intercepts are (−8, 0) and (0, 4).
The intersection of the two boundary lines is found from x = y + 4 and 2y − (y + 4) = 8, so y = 12 and x = 16.
In the first quadrant, the feasible region has corner points (0, 0), (4, 0), (16, 12) and (0, 4).
Thus, the maximum is at the corner point (16, 12).

explain.title: Constraints and decision variables
explain.body: While tackling a certain problem from everyday life each linear inequality concerning the problem is named as problem constraint. The system of linear inequalities involved in the problem concerned is called problem constraints. The variables used in the system of linear inequalities relating to the problems of everyday life are non-negative and are called non-negative constraints. These non-negative constraints play an important role for taking decision. So, these variables are called decision variables.

explain.title: Feasible region and feasible solution
explain.body: A region which is restricted to the first quadrant is referred to as a feasible region for the set of given constraints. Each point of the feasible region is called a feasible solution of the system of linear inequalities (or for the set of a given constraints). A point of a solution region where two of its boundary lines intersect, is called a corner point or vertex of the solution region.

explain.title: Objective and optimal solutions
explain.body: A function which is to be maximized or minimized is called an objective function. The feasible solution which maximizes or minimizes the objective function is called the optimal solution.

explain.title: How to find the best value
explain.body: Graph the solution set of linear inequality constraints to determine feasible region. Find the corner points of the feasible region. Evaluate the objective function at each corner point to find the optimal solution.

explain.title: Linear equations
explain.body: A linear equation has an equals sign and a variable of degree 1. Solve it by using inverse operations to isolate the variable. For example, 5x − 10 = 10 gives x = 4.

explain.title: Linear inequalities
explain.body: An inequality uses signs such as <, >, ≤, or ≥. Solve by isolating the variable and keep the inequality direction correct. A strict inequality such as x < 3 does not include 3.

explain.title: Boundary lines and half planes
explain.body: The equation formed from a linear inequality is called the associated equation. Its line divides the plane into two half planes; the inequality tells which side satisfies the condition.

explain.title: Feasible region and vertices
explain.body: The feasible region is the region that satisfies all the constraints. Its corner points are also called vertices.

explain.title: Objective function
explain.body: A function that is to be maximized or minimized is called the objective function. Check its value at each corner point of the feasible region, then choose the greatest value for a maximum or the least for a minimum.

definitions.text: An equation of the form ax + b = 0 where ‘a’ and ‘b’ are constants, a ≠ 0 and ‘x’ is a variable, is called a linear equation in one variable. In linear equation, the highest power of the variable is always 1.

definitions.term: General form of linear equation in one variable
definitions.text: ax + b = 0 and a ≠ 0 is also called the general form of linear equation in one variable.

definitions.term: Solving a linear equation in one variable
definitions.text: Solving a linear equation in one variable means finding the value of the variable that makes the equation true. To solve the equation, the goal is to isolate the variable on one side of the equation and determine its value.

definitions.term: Operations that do not change the order of an inequality
definitions.text: The following operations will not affect the order of inequality while changing it to simpler equivalent form: (i) Adding or subtracting a constant to each side of it. ii) Multiplying or dividing each side by a positive constant.

definitions.term: Effect of multiplying or dividing by a negative constant
definitions.text: The order of an inequality is changed by multiplying or dividing each side by a negative constant.

Generally, a linear inequality in two variables x and y can be one of the following forms: ax + by < c;  ax + by > c;  ax + by ≤ c;  ax + by ≥ c Where a, b, c are constants and a, b are not both zero.
The regions (i) and (ii) are called half planes and the line ax + by = c is called the boundary of each half plane.

definitions.term: Solution of a linear inequality in x and y
definitions.text: A solution of a linear inequality in x and y is an ordered pair of numbers which satisfies the inequality.
Note that the linear equation ax + by = c is called "associated or corresponding equation" of each of the above-mentioned inequalities.

definitions.term: Solution region for a system of linear inequalities
definitions.text: The graph of a system of linear inequalities consists of the set of all ordered pairs (x, y) in the xy-plane which simultaneously satisfies all the inequalities in the system. To find the graph of such a system, we draw the graph of each inequality in the system on the same coordinate axes and then take intersection of all the graphs. The common region so obtained is called the solution region for the system of inequalities.

fullMarks: For a one-variable equation, show the same operation on both sides when adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing; then state the value of x clearly.
For an inequality, reverse the inequality sign whenever you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number.
On a real number line, use an open circle for < or > and a filled circle for ≤ or ≥; draw the ray in the correct direction.
For a graph in the xy-plane, first write the associated equation, find two points (often the intercepts), and draw the boundary accurately.
Use a dashed boundary for < or > and a solid boundary for ≤ or ≥, because equality means points on the line are included.
Test a point not on the boundary, usually (0, 0), in the original inequality; show whether it satisfies the inequality and shade the correct side.
For a system, graph every inequality on the same labelled axes and shade only the common region that satisfies all inequalities.
mistakes: Mistake: Keeping the inequality sign the same after dividing or multiplying by a negative number. Fix: Reverse the sign every time you do this.
Mistake: Using a filled circle for a strict inequality or an open circle for an inequality that includes equality. Fix: Use open for < or > and filled for ≤ or ≥.
Mistake: Drawing a solid line for every inequality. Fix: Use a dashed line for < or >, and a solid line for ≤ or ≥.

Mistake: Shading the side of a boundary line without checking it. Fix: Substitute a test point not on the line into the original inequality; shade its side if it works, otherwise shade the opposite side.
Mistake: Reversing the x- and y-intercepts. Fix: Set y = 0 to find the x-intercept and x = 0 to find the y-intercept; write each point in (x, y) order.
Mistake: For a system, shading the union of the two regions or leaving both full regions shaded. Fix: The solution is only the overlap that satisfies both inequalities.
Mistake: Losing a negative sign while removing brackets or combining fractions. Fix: Distribute signs carefully and check the final value in the original equation or inequality.

explain.title: Angles in standard position
explain.body: The angle is said to be in standard position if: (a) Its vertex is located at the origin of the coordinate plane. (b) One of its rays (the initial side) lies along the positive x-axis. The other ray is the terminal side.

explain.title: Positive, negative, and co-terminal angles
explain.body: A positive angle turns counterclockwise from its initial side; a negative angle turns clockwise. Co-terminal angles have the same initial and terminal sides and differ by a multiple of 360° or 2π rad.

explain.title: Degree and DMS measures
explain.body: A degree is 1/360th of a full rotation. Also, 1° = 60′ and 1′ = 60″. To change decimal degrees to DMS, multiply the decimal part by 60 for minutes, then multiply any leftover decimal part by 60 for seconds.

explain.title: Radian measure and conversions
explain.body: A radian is a unit of angular measure in mathematics, particularly in trigonometry. It is defined as, “the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius of the circle”. A full circle is 2π radians = 360°. Use 1° = π/180 rad and 1 rad = 180°/π.

explain.title: Arc length and sector area
explain.body: When θ is in radians, arc length is ℓ = rθ and area of sector is A = 1/2 r²θ. If the angle is given in degrees, convert it to radians before using these formulas.

For a triangle-ratio question, marks are earned for identifying the correct sides and writing the correct ratio, then simplifying it correctly.

explain.title: Name the sides from the chosen angle
explain.body: The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse. From the chosen acute angle, the side across from it is the perpendicular, and the side beside it (not the hypotenuse) is the base.

explain.title: Use the textbook's definitions
explain.body:
For this right angled triangle ACB, the trigonometric ratios of an angle “θ” are defined as:

sin θ = Perpendicular/Hypotenuse = a/c : cosec θ = Hypotenuse/Perpendicular = c/a
cos θ = Base/Hypotenuse = b/c : sec θ = Hypotenuse/Base = c/b
tan θ = Perpendicular/Base = a/b : cot θ = Base/Perpendicular = b/a

explain.title: Remember the reciprocal ratios
explain.body:
NOTE:

(i) cosec θ = 1/sin θ

(ii) sec θ = 1/cos θ

(iii) cot θ = 1/tan θ

explain.title: Relate tangent to sine and cosine
explain.body: The textbook shows that tan θ = (a/c)/(b/c), so tan θ = sin θ/cos θ. Similarly, cot θ = cos θ/sin θ.

explain.title: Use complementary angles
explain.body: The textbook states: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ; cos(90° − θ) = sin θ; tan(90° − θ) = cot θ; cot(90° − θ) = tan θ; sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ; cosec(90° − θ) = sec θ.

mistakes: Choosing the opposite and adjacent sides without checking which angle is being used.
Using the hypotenuse as the base or perpendicular; the hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle.
Reversing a ratio, for example writing sin θ as hypotenuse/perpendicular instead of perpendicular/hypotenuse.
Forgetting that sec, cosec and cot are reciprocal ratios.
Mixing up complementary identities, such as writing sin(90° − θ) = sin θ instead of cos θ.
In a verification question, stating the result without showing the ratios and multiplication.

explain.title: The three fundamental identities
explain.body: The Pythagoras theorem says: “The square of the length of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is equal to the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides”. Dividing a² + b² = c² by c², b² and a² gives sin² θ + cos² θ = 1, tan² θ + 1 = sec² θ, and 1 + cot² θ = cosec² θ. These are called Pythagoras identities.

explain.title: Finding ratios from one given ratio
explain.body: Make a right triangle using the given ratio, then find its missing side using the Pythagoras theorem. Since θ lies in the first quadrant, the side lengths and the trigonometric ratios are positive. Use the side definitions to find the ratios and their reciprocals.

explain.title: Proving an identity
explain.body: An identity proof uses equal expressions to change one side into the other. Start with L.H.S or R.H.S, show each algebraic step, and use the trigonometric identities or ratio definitions where needed. Stop when the expression matches the other side.

mistakes: Confusing the side positions: sin θ = perpendicular/hypotenuse, cos θ = base/hypotenuse, and tan θ = perpendicular/base.
Forgetting to take the positive square root for a side when θ lies in the first quadrant.
Changing both sides of an identity at once without showing that the expressions remain equal.
Using sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 incorrectly; for example, replacing sin² θ by 1 − cos² θ is valid, but replacing it by 1 − cos θ is not.
Forgetting to square both terms when expanding a squared expression, or losing the middle term in a binomial expansion.

explain.body: In the textbook's square, each side is 1 and the diagonal is √2. The trigonometric ratios are: sin 45° = a/c = 1/√2 ; cosec 45° = c/a = √2; cos 45° = b/c = 1/√2 ; sec 45° = c/b = √2; tan 45° = a/b = 1 ; cot 45° = b/a = 1.

explain.title: The 30° and 60° triangle
explain.body: The perpendicular bisector of an equilateral triangle with side 2 makes a right triangle with sides 1, √3 and 2. The textbook gives: sin 30° = 1/2 ; cosec 30° = 2; cos 30° = √3/2 ; sec 30° = 2/√3; tan 30° = 1/√3 ; cot 30° = √3. For 60°: sin 60° = √3/2 ; cos 60° = 1/2 ; tan 60° = √3; cosec 60° = 2/√3 ; sec 60° = 2 ; cot 60° = 1/√3.

explain.title: Read the special-angle table
explain.body: These results in the form of a table can be written as: θ: 0°, 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2. sin θ: 0, 1/2, 1/√2, √3/2, 1. cos θ: 1, √3/2, 1/√2, 1/2, 0. tan θ: 0, 1/√3, 1, √3, ∞.

explain.title: Radian angles match special degree angles
explain.body: Use π/6 = 30°, π/4 = 45° and π/3 = 60°. For example, tan π/6 = tan 30° = 1/√3 = √3/3.

steps: Draw an equilateral triangle ABC with each side 2 units.
Draw AD perpendicular to BC; then D is the midpoint of BC.

Substituting the known lengths gives the exact value.

mistakes: Measuring an angle of elevation or depression from the vertical instead of from the horizontal.
Using the wrong sides in the tangent ratio; tangent is opposite/adjacent.
Treating the sloping line as the horizontal distance, or vice versa.
Forgetting that the angle of depression equals the corresponding angle at the ground when the horizontal lines are parallel.
Leaving out units or rounding the final answer too early.

solutions.question: The angle of elevation of the top of a pole 40 m high is 60° when seen from a point on the ground level. Find the distance of the point from the foot of the pole.
steps: In the triangle ABC, we have
Let mA̅B̅ = x (the point B is the foot of the pole BC)
(Figure: Right-angled triangle ABC with AB = x m, BC = 40 m, ∠A = 60°, and an arrow labelled “Angle of elevation” pointing toward AC.)
Hence, distance of the point from the foot of the pole = 23.09 m
why: Naming the triangle sets up the right-triangle relationship.
The pole's height is the vertical side of the triangle.
The angle of elevation is measured from the horizontal ground.
We call the unknown horizontal distance x.
The pole and ground meet at a right angle.
The diagram shows how the height, distance, and angle form a triangle.
Tangent relates the opposite side to the adjacent side.
We substitute the height and the unknown distance.
Rearranging isolates the horizontal distance.
We evaluate the quotient to get a decimal distance.
This states the requested distance from the pole's foot.

steps: In the triangle ABC, AB is the tower and point C is the position of man. We have
(Figure: Right-angled triangle ABC with AB = 30 m and BC = x m; ∠C = 45°. A horizontal line from A to D and an arrow are labelled “Angle of depression”; ∠CAD = 45°.)
Let x be the base of right angled triangle ABC,
Hence, man is 30 m far from the tower.
why: Naming the vertices sets up a right triangle model for the tower and man's positions.
The tower height is the vertical side given in the question.
The angle of depression equals the ground angle by alternate interior angles.
The ground distance is the unknown we need to calculate.
The diagram represents the height, horizontal distance, and matching 45° angle.
Naming the unknown base gives a variable for the distance sought.
Tangent uses opposite over adjacent, matching the height and ground distance.
Since tan 45° equals 1, substitute the known height and unknown distance.
Multiply both sides by x to isolate the distance.
This states the calculated ground distance in context.

why: Representing the unknown height by h makes it possible to form an equation.
Tangent relates the opposite height to the adjacent 40-metre distance.
Use the known exact value of tan 60°.
Multiply by 40 to isolate h.
Substitute a decimal approximation for √3 to estimate the height.

solutions.figure: An isosceles triangle with vertex angle 120° and base 10 cm. Its altitude bisects the base into two 5 cm segments and the vertex angle into two 60° angles.
why: Naming h identifies the altitude we need to calculate.
An isosceles triangle's altitude bisects its base into equal halves.
Tangent relates the half-base opposite 60° to the altitude.
We replace tan 60° with its exact value.
Rearranging isolates the altitude.
We approximate √3 to calculate a decimal answer.
This gives the altitude rounded to two decimal places.

solutions.figure: A right-angled triangle formed by the tree, the ground and the line of sight. The tree’s height is 72 m, the horizontal distance is 100 m and the angle of elevation is θ.

steps: Let the length of the ladder be l m.
solutions.figure: A right-angled triangle formed by the wall, the ground and the ladder. The ladder makes an angle of 60° with the ground and reaches 10 m up the wall; its length is l.
why: Naming l identifies the ladder length we need.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, matching height and ladder.
We substitute the exact value of sin 60°.
Rearranging isolates the ladder length.
We use a decimal approximation to evaluate the radical.
This gives the ladder length to two decimal places.

solutions.question: A light house tower is 150 m high from the sea level. The angle of depression from the top of the tower to a ship is 60°. Find the distance between the ship and the tower.
steps: Let the horizontal distance between the ship and the tower be x m.
The angle of elevation from the ship to the top of the tower is 60° (alternate angles).
solutions.figure: A right-angled triangle formed by the lighthouse tower, sea level and the line of sight to the ship. The tower height is 150 m, the angle of depression is 60° and the horizontal distance to the ship is x.
why: Naming x identifies the horizontal distance we need.
Parallel sea-level lines make the depression and elevation angles equal.
Tangent relates tower height to the horizontal distance.
We substitute the exact value of tan 60°.
Rearranging isolates the horizontal distance.
We approximate the radical to calculate the distance.

solutions.question: Measure of an angle of elevation of the top of a pole is 15° from a point on the ground, in walking 100 m towards the pole the measure of angle is found to be 30°. Find the height of the pole.
steps: Let the height of the pole be h m and the distance from the nearer point to its foot be x m.
At the nearer point, tan 30° = h/x, so x = h cot 30°.
The farther point is 100 m away, so tan 15° = h/(x + 100), giving x + 100 = h cot 15°.
Subtract the two distance expressions: 100 = h(cot 15° − cot 30°).
solutions.answer: 49.98 m (the book’s numerical value is 49.98; the unit for the height should be m, not °).
solutions.figure: A pole of height h stands vertically on the ground. Two observation points lie on the same straight ground line on one side of the pole, 100 m apart. The angles of elevation from the farther and nearer points are 15° and 30°, respectively.
accept: 49.98 m (the book’s numerical value is 49.98; the unit for the height should be m, not °).
solutions.note: Your textbook's answer key shows 49.98°. The height is a length, so its unit must be metres, not degrees. Solving gives 50 m exactly; using rounded trigonometric-table values gives approximately 49.98 m, so the textbook's answer key has the wrong unit.
