solutions.answer: The angle of elevation of the Sun is 33.69°.
solutions.figure: Draw a vertical tower AB of height 300 m and a horizontal shadow BC of length 450 m. Join A to C. Mark the right angle at B and the angle of elevation θ at C.
why: Naming θ identifies the angle we need to find.
The tower and shadow form a right triangle with these side lengths.
Tangent uses the opposite height and adjacent shadow.
Substitution and reduction simplify the tangent ratio.
Inverse tangent converts the ratio into an angle.
Rounding gives the angle of elevation.

solutions.question: Measure of angle of elevation of the top of a cliff is 25°, on walking 100 metres towards the cliff, measure of angle of elevation of the top is 45°. Find the height of the cliff.
steps: Let the height of the cliff be h m and the distance of the farther observation point from the foot of the cliff be x m.
The distance of the nearer observation point from the foot of the cliff is (x − 100) m.
Using the angle of elevation 25°, tan 25° = h / x.
Using the angle of elevation 45°, tan 45° = h / (x − 100).
Substituting x = h cot 25°, h cot 25° − 100 = h.
solutions.answer: The height of the cliff is 87.4 m.
solutions.figure: Draw a vertical cliff AB of height h and a horizontal ground line through its foot B. Mark two observation points C and D on the ground, with D 100 m closer to B than C. Join A to C and A to D. Mark the angles of elevation at C as 25° and at D as 45°, and the right angle at B.
why: Naming h and x represents the unknown height and farther distance.
Walking 100 m closer reduces the distance by 100 m.
Tangent relates the height to the farther horizontal distance.
Rearranging expresses the farther distance using cotangent.
Tangent relates height and distance at the nearer point.
Since tan 45° is one, the two sides are equal.
Substitution removes x so the equation has only h.
Factoring h makes the height easier to isolate.
Dividing isolates the unknown height.
Using the cotangent approximation gives the height in metres.

solutions.question: From the top of a hill 300 m high, the measure of the angle of depression of a point on the nearer shore of the river is 70° and measure of the angle of depression of a point, directly across the river is 50°. Find the width of the river How far is the river from the foot of the hill?
steps: Let the distance from the foot of the hill to the nearer shore be BC = x m, and let the width of the river be CD = w m.
The angle of depression to the nearer shore equals the angle of elevation at C, so ∠ACB = 70°.
In right triangle ABC, tan 70° = AB / BC = 300 / x.
The angle of depression to the point directly across the river equals the angle of elevation at D, so ∠ADB = 50°.
The horizontal distance from B to D is BC + CD = x + w.
In right triangle ABD, tan 50° = AB / BD = 300 / (x + w).
solutions.answer: The width of the river is 142.5 m, and the river is 109.2 m from the foot of the hill.
solutions.figure: Draw the hill vertically as AB = 300 m, with B on a horizontal line representing the nearer shore. Mark the nearer shore point C and the point D directly across the river from C. Join A to C and A to D. Mark the angles of depression from the horizontal through A as 70° to C and 50° to D. Mark the right angles at B and C. Label BC as the distance from the hill to the river and CD as the river width.
why: Naming x and w distinguishes the shore distance from the river width.
Equal alternate angles transfer the depression angle to the ground triangle.
Tangent relates the hill's height to the nearer horizontal distance.
Rearranging gives the shore distance, then approximation gives metres.
The same parallel-line angle rule gives the angle at the far shore.
The total horizontal distance includes both shore distance and river width.
Tangent relates the hill height to this total distance.
Rearranging finds the total horizontal distance.
Subtracting the nearer distance leaves the river's width.

steps: Let the height of the kite above the hand be KB = h m.
In right triangle HBK, HK = 120 m and ∠KHB = 50°.
solutions.answer: The kite is 91.92 m above the hand holding it.

why: Naming the unknown height lets us represent the answer with a variable.
The string is the hypotenuse, and the angle is measured from the horizontal.
Sine means opposite side divided by hypotenuse in a right triangle.
Rearranging the sine equation isolates the height.
Using the calculator value of sine gives the height in metres.

explain.title: Convert degrees and radians
explain.body: Use 180° = π radians. To change degrees to radians, multiply by π/180°. To change radians to degrees, multiply by 180°/π. For example, 255° = 255π/180 = 17π/12 radians.

explain.title: Use trigonometric ratios in a right triangle
explain.body: For an angle θ, sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, and tan θ = opposite/adjacent. Choose the ratio that uses the known side and the unknown side.

explain.title: Use reciprocal ratios and identities
explain.body: The reciprocal ratios are cosec θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ and cot θ = 1/tan θ. Useful identities include sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 and sec² θ − tan² θ = 1.

explain.title: Prove an identity by simplifying
explain.body: Work on one side at a time. Replace tan, cot, sec or cosec with expressions in sine and cosine, use known identities, and simplify until that side matches the other side.

explain.title: Solve elevation and ladder problems
explain.body: Mark the angle, height and horizontal distance on the right triangle. An angle of elevation is measured up from the horizontal. A ladder is the hypotenuse; use sine for the height opposite its ground angle.

mistakes: Using π/180° when converting radians to degrees, or 180°/π when converting degrees to radians.
Confusing the opposite and adjacent sides in an elevation triangle.
Using the ladder length as a side other than the hypotenuse.
Forgetting to square both sine and cosine in sin² θ + cos² θ = 1.
Starting an identity proof by changing both sides at once, making the equality hard to justify.
Leaving off units or rounding the final distance or height incorrectly.

solutions.question: Prove the following trigonometric identities: (sin θ)/(1 − cos θ) = (1 + cos θ)/sin θ
steps: = [sin θ(1 + cos θ)]/[(1 − cos θ)(1 + cos θ)]
solutions.answer: (sin θ)/(1 − cos θ) = (1 + cos θ)/sin θ
why: Begin with the left-hand side so we can transform it into the right-hand side.
Multiply by the conjugate to remove the difference of squares in the denominator.
Use the difference of squares rule: (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b².
Use the identity sin² θ + cos² θ = 1, so 1 − cos² θ = sin² θ.
Cancel the common factor sin θ, assuming the expressions are defined.
The expression now matches the right-hand side, proving the identity.

solutions.question: Prove the following trigonometric identities: sin θ (cosec θ − sin θ) = 1/sec² θ
steps: L.H.S. = sin θ(cosec θ − sin θ)
solutions.answer: sin θ (cosec θ − sin θ) = 1/sec² θ
why: Begin with the left-hand side so we can transform it into the right-hand side.
Replace cosec θ with its reciprocal definition, 1/sin θ.
Distribute sin θ across the brackets and simplify.
Use the identity 1 − sin² θ = cos² θ.
Use sec θ = 1/cos θ, so 1/sec² θ = cos² θ.
The expression now matches the right-hand side, proving the identity.

solutions.question: Prove the following trigonometric identities: (cosec θ − sec θ)/(cosec θ + sec θ) = (1 − tan θ)/(1 + tan θ)
steps: L.H.S. = (cosec θ − sec θ)/(cosec θ + sec θ)
= [(cos θ − sin θ)/(sin θ cos θ)]/[(cos θ + sin θ)/(sin θ cos θ)]
= (cos θ − sin θ)/(cos θ + sin θ)
solutions.answer: (cosec θ − sec θ)/(cosec θ + sec θ) = (1 − tan θ)/(1 + tan θ)
why: Begin with the left-hand side so we can transform it into the right-hand side.
Replace cosec and sec with their reciprocal definitions.
Combine each pair of fractions using a common denominator.
The common denominators cancel in the division.
Divide the numerator and denominator by cos θ to obtain tangent ratios.
The expression now matches the right-hand side, proving the identity.

solutions.question: Prove the following trigonometric identities: tan θ + cot θ = 1/(sin θ cos θ)
steps: = sin θ/cos θ + cos θ/sin θ
= (sin² θ + cos² θ)/(sin θ cos θ)
solutions.answer: tan θ + cot θ = 1/(sin θ cos θ)
why: Begin with the left-hand side so we can transform it into the right-hand side.
Replace tangent and cotangent with their sine and cosine ratios.
Use a common denominator to add the fractions.
Use sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 in the numerator.
The expression now matches the right-hand side, proving the identity.

solutions.question: Prove the following trigonometric identities: (cos θ + sin θ)/(cos θ − sin θ) + (cos θ − sin θ)/(cos θ + sin θ) = 2/(1 − 2 sin² θ)
steps: L.H.S. = (cos θ + sin θ)/(cos θ − sin θ) + (cos θ − sin θ)/(cos θ + sin θ)
= [(cos θ + sin θ)² + (cos θ − sin θ)²]/[(cos θ − sin θ)(cos θ + sin θ)]
solutions.answer: (cos θ + sin θ)/(cos θ − sin θ) + (cos θ − sin θ)/(cos θ + sin θ) = 2/(1 − 2 sin² θ)
why: Begin with the left-hand side so we can transform it into the right-hand side.
Add the fractions using a common denominator.
Expand the squares and combine like terms in the numerator and denominator.
Use sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 to simplify the numerator.
Use cos² θ = 1 − sin² θ to rewrite the denominator.
The expression now matches the right-hand side, proving the identity.

solutions.question: Prove the following trigonometric identities: (1 + cos θ)/(1 − cos θ) = (cosec θ + cot θ)²
steps: = (1 + cos θ)²/[(1 − cos θ)(1 + cos θ)]
solutions.answer: (1 + cos θ)/(1 − cos θ) = (cosec θ + cot θ)²
why: We start from the right-hand side to transform it into the left-hand side.
The reciprocal and quotient identities express cosecant and cotangent using sine and cosine.
A common denominator lets us combine the two fractions.
Squaring a fraction squares both its numerator and denominator.
The identity sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ factors the denominator.
The common factor 1 + cos θ cancels, where the expressions are defined.
This matches the left-hand side, proving the identity.

definitions.text: A plane figure which is formed by two rays sharing a common end point is called an angle. The two rays are known as the sides of the angle. The common end point is known as vertex. The amount of rotation or measure of opening between these rays is called an angle.

The angle is said to be in standard position if:
(a) Its vertex is located at the origin of the coordinate plane.
(b) One of its rays (the initial side) lies along the positive x-axis.
Co-terminal angles are angles that share the same initial side and terminal side in standard position, but they may have different measures. These angles differ by a multiple of 360° or 2π rad.
A degree (°) is a unit of measurement of an angle. It represents (1/360)th of a full rotation around a point. In simpler terms, a degree is the measure of an angle, with a complete circle being 360°.

A radian is a unit of angular measure in mathematics, particularly in trigonometry. It is defined as, “the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius of the circle”. Unlike degrees, which are based on dividing a circle into 360 parts, the radian is inherently related to the circle's geometry and arc length.

The identities (ii), (iii) and (iv) are known as Pythagoras identities.
Finding the measures of the remaining elements is called the solution of a triangle Here we learn the solution of a right angled triangle only.

fullMarks: For angle conversions, show the conversion factor and the cancellation: multiply degrees by π/180 or radians by 180/π. Keep exact answers in terms of π when asked.
For DMS conversions, show the minutes ÷ 60 and seconds ÷ 3600 parts separately before adding them.
For a sector problem, convert the central angle to radians first, write ℓ = rθ or A = 1/2 × r² × θ, and give the correct final units: cm or cm².
For a right-triangle ratio, identify the opposite side, adjacent side and hypotenuse with respect to the stated angle before substituting values.
For an identity proof, begin with L.H.S. or R.H.S., show one valid algebraic step per line, name the identity used when helpful, and finish by stating that L.H.S. = R.H.S.

mistakes: Using 60 instead of 60 × 60 when converting a decimal degree to seconds. Fix: convert the decimal part of the minutes by multiplying by 60.
Forgetting to change degrees into radians before using ℓ = rθ or A = 1/2 × r² × θ. Fix: convert first and show the radian angle.
Mixing up the opposite and adjacent sides when the reference angle changes. Fix: mark the chosen angle and identify its opposite and adjacent sides again.
Writing sec θ = 1 ÷ sin θ or cosec θ = 1 ÷ cos θ. Fix: sec is reciprocal of cosine; cosec is reciprocal of sine.
Dropping the square when using a Pythagorean identity, such as writing sin θ + cos θ = 1. Fix: keep the squares: sin² θ + cos² θ = 1.
Starting an identity proof by changing both sides at once. Fix: work from one side only until it becomes the other side.
Giving a sector length in square units or a sector area in ordinary units. Fix: arc length uses units such as cm; area uses square units such as cm².

shortTheory.question: Define an angle.
shortTheory.answer: A plane figure which is formed by two rays sharing a common end point is called an angle. The two rays are known as the sides of the angle. The common end point is known as vertex.

shortTheory.question: When is an angle in standard position?
shortTheory.answer:
The angle is said to be in standard position if:
(a) Its vertex is located at the origin of the coordinate plane.
(b) One of its rays (the initial side) lies along the positive x-axis.

shortTheory.question: What are co-terminal angles?
shortTheory.answer: Co-terminal angles are angles that share the same initial side and terminal side in standard position, but they may have different measures. These angles differ by a multiple of 360° or 2π rad.

shortTheory.question: Define a radian.
shortTheory.answer: A radian is a unit of angular measure in mathematics, particularly in trigonometry. It is defined as, “the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius of the circle”.

shortTheory.question: State Pythagoras Theorem.
shortTheory.answer: The square of the length of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is equal to the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides.

shortTheory.question: What is meant by the solution of a triangle?
shortTheory.answer: Finding the measures of the remaining elements is called the solution of a triangle Here we learn the solution of a right angled triangle only.

explain.title: The coordinate plane
explain.body: Draw two perpendicular number lines that meet at the origin O. The horizontal line x'Ox is called the x-axis and the vertical line y'Oy is called the y-axis. A point is named by an ordered pair (x, y).

explain.title: Coordinates and quadrants
explain.body: The first component of the ordered pair (x, y) is called x-coordinate or abscissa and the second component is called y-coordinate or ordinate of P. In Quadrant I both coordinates are positive; in II x is negative and y positive; in III both are negative; in IV x is positive and y negative. Points on the x-axis have the form (a, 0), and points on the y-axis have the form (0, b).

explain.title: Distance between two points
explain.body: For A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂), the distance formula is d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). Subtract matching coordinates, square the differences, add them, and take the square root. Distance is always non-negative.

explain.title: Midpoint of a line segment
explain.body: The midpoint is halfway between two endpoints. Average the x-coordinates to get its x-coordinate and average the y-coordinates to get its y-coordinate: M(x, y) = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).

explain.title: Inclination and slope
explain.body: The textbook defines inclination this way: “The angle α (0° < α < 180°) is measured counterclockwise from positive x-axis to a non-horizontal straight line ℓ is called the inclination of ℓ.” The textbook also defines slope this way: “In analytical geometry, slope or gradient m of a non-vertical straight line with α as its inclination is defined by: m = tan α.” A horizontal line has slope zero; a vertical line has an undefined slope.

explain.title: Slope from two points
explain.body: For points P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂), use m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Subtract the y-coordinates in the same order as the x-coordinates. The textbook states: “If slope of AB = slope of BC, then the points A, B and C are collinear.”

explain.title: Parallel and perpendicular lines
explain.body: Two lines are parallel when their slopes are equal. They are perpendicular when m₁m₂ = −1, so their slopes are negative reciprocals.

explain.title: Choose an equation form
explain.body: Use y = mx + c when the slope and y-intercept are known. Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) when a point and slope are known. Use x/a + y/b = 1 when the x- and y-intercepts are known. A horizontal line has equation y = a, and a vertical line has equation x = b.

explain.title: General equation
explain.body: The general equation of a straight line is ax + by + c = 0, where a and b are not simultaneously zero. Rearranging it to y = mx + c₁ reveals its slope when b is not zero.

definitions.text: The two lines are called coordinate axes. The horizontal line x'Ox is called the x-axis and the vertical line y'Oy is called the y-axis.
The first component of the ordered pair (x, y) is called x-coordinate or abscissa and the second component is called y-coordinate or ordinate of P.

definitions.term: Two dimensional rectangular (or Cartesian) coordinate system
definitions.text: This method of pairing off in a one-to-one fashion the points in a plane with ordered pairs of real numbers is called the two dimensional rectangular (or Cartesian) coordinate system.

The coordinate axes divide the plane into four equal parts called quadrants. They are defined as follows:

Quadrant I: All points (x, y) with x > 0, y > 0

Quadrant II: All points (x, y) with x < 0, y > 0

Quadrant III:All points (x, y) with x < 0, y < 0

Quadrant IV:All points (x, y) with x > 0, y < 0
The point P in the plane that corresponds to an ordered pair (x, y) is called the graph.
The points on x-axis are of the form (a, 0) and the points on y-axis are of the form (0, b).
The distance is always taken to be non-negative. It is not a directed distance from A to B.

The midpoint formula is used in geometry to find central point between two given points in a coordinate plane. This formula is particularly useful when you need to divide a line segment into two equal halves or parts.
The angle α (0° < α < 180°) is measured counterclockwise from positive x-axis to a non-horizontal straight line ℓ is called the inclination of ℓ.

The measure of steepness (ratio of rise to the run) is termed as slope or gradient of the inclined path and is denoted by m.

m = rise/run = y/x = tan α
In analytical geometry, slope or gradient m of a non-vertical straight line with α as its inclination is defined by: m = tan α.

If a non-vertical line ℓ with inclination α passes through two points P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂), then the slope or gradient m of ℓ is given by

m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = tan α
If ℓ is horizontal, its slope is zero and if ℓ is vertical then its slope is undefined.
If slope of AB = slope of BC, then the points A, B and C are collinear.

The two lines ℓ₁ and ℓ₂ with slopes m₁ and m₂ respectively are:

(i) parallel iff m₁ = m₂

(ii) perpendicular iff m₁ = −1/m₂

or m₁m₂ = −1

All the points on the line ℓ parallel to x-axis remain at a constant distance (say a) from x-axis. Therefore, each point on the line has its distance from x-axis equal to a, which is its y-coordinate (ordinate). So, all the points on this line satisfy the equation: y = a

All the points on the line ℓ parallel to y-axis remain at a constant distance (say b) from y-axis. Each point on the line has its distance from y-axis equal to b, which is its x-coordinate (abscissa). So, all the points on this line satisfy the equation: x = b

Equation of a non-vertical straight line with slope m and y-intercept c is given by:

y = mx + c

Equation of a non-vertical straight line ℓ with slope m and passing through a point Q (x₁, y₁) is given by:

y − y₁ = m (x − x₁)

We have m = (y − y₁)/(x − x₁) = tan α, where α is the inclination of the line.

(y − y₁)/(x − x₁) = sin α/cos α or (x − x₁)/cos α = (y − y₁)/sin α = r(say)

This is called symmetric form of equation of the line.

Equation of a non-vertical straight line passing through two points Q(x₁, y₁) and R(x₂, y₂) is:

y − y₁ = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)(x − x₁)

or

y − y₂ = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)(x − x₂)

Equation of a line whose non-zero x and y-intercepts are a and b respectively is:

x/a + y/b = 1

An equation of a non-vertical straight-line ℓ, such that length of the perpendicular from the origin to ℓ is p and α is the inclination of this perpendicular, is

x cos α + y sin α = p

fullMarks: For a distance question, write the distance formula first, substitute both coordinates with brackets, simplify the squares, and give the non-negative answer. Add units when the question gives units.
For a midpoint, show the average of the x-coordinates and the average of the y-coordinates separately, then write the ordered pair in brackets.
For slope questions, state which points are (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), substitute carefully, and include the inclination if asked. State that a vertical line has undefined slope.

For collinearity, calculate two slopes using a shared point and finish by stating that equal slopes show the three points are collinear.
For a line equation, identify the given point, slope, intercept, or intercepts first; use the matching form, simplify, and state that the resulting equation is required.

mistakes: Using the same sign order in the numerator and the opposite sign order in the denominator when calculating slope. Fix: use (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), keeping each point's coordinates together.
Treating a vertical line as having slope zero. Fix: horizontal lines have slope zero; vertical lines have undefined slope.
Forgetting brackets around negative coordinates in distance calculations. Fix: substitute a negative coordinate in parentheses before squaring.
Dividing only one coordinate by 2 in the midpoint formula. Fix: average x-coordinates together and y-coordinates together.
Claiming lines are perpendicular because their slopes are negative, without checking the product. Fix: show m₁m₂ = −1.
Using y = mx + c for a vertical line. Fix: a vertical line has equation x = b, where b is its fixed x-coordinate.
Giving an equation without a concluding statement or leaving a distance without units when units are given. Fix: state the required result clearly and include the correct units.

shortTheory.answer:

ax + by + c = 0 ...(i)

The equation (i) represents a straight line and is called the general equation of a straight line.

explain.title: What is a statement?
explain.body: A sentence or mathematical expression which may be true or false but not both is called a statement. For example, 3 + 4 = 8 is a statement, and it is false.

explain.title: True and false statements
explain.body: A mathematical statement has one truth value: true or false. “The sum of the measures of the interior angles of a triangle is 180°” is true; “The set of integers is finite” is false.

explain.title: Induction and deduction
explain.body: Induction draws a general conclusion from a limited number of observations or repeated experiments. Deduction draws a conclusion from accepted or well-known facts.

explain.title: Axiom, conjecture and theorem
explain.body: An axiom is accepted as true without proof. A conjecture is proposed as true but has not been proved. A theorem is established by proof. Your textbook treats the straight-line fact as an axiom, the even-number-and-primes claim as a conjecture, and the triangle angle result as a theorem.

explain.title: How to prove an algebraic identity
explain.body: To show L.H.S. = R.H.S., start with one side, usually L.H.S., simplify one step at a time, and finish by reaching R.H.S. For example, expand squares and then combine like terms.

mistakes: Calling a question or command a statement: it does not assert something that is true or false.
Mixing up induction and deduction: observations and experiments suggest induction; accepted facts leading to a conclusion show deduction.

Cancelling terms across addition or subtraction instead of factoring first.

explain.title: Negation: ~
explain.body: Your textbook reads ~p as “Not p, negation of p.” It changes a statement to its opposite: if p is true, ~p is false.

explain.title: Conjunction: ∧
explain.body: Your textbook reads p ∧ q as “p and q.” It is true only when both p and q are true.

explain.title: Disjunction: ∨
explain.body: Your textbook reads p ∨ q as “p or q.” It is true when at least one of p or q is true.

explain.title: Conditional: →
explain.body: Your textbook reads p → q as “If p then q, p implies q.” It is false only when p is true and q is false.

explain.title: Equivalence: ↔
explain.body: Your textbook reads p ↔ q as “p if and only if q, p is equivalent to q.” It is true when p and q have the same truth value.

solutions.question: Prove the following statements: If x is an odd integer, then show that it x² − 4x + 6 is odd.
steps: Let x be an odd integer.
Then x = 2k + 1 for some integer k.
Since 2k² − 2k + 1 is an integer, x² − 4x + 6 is odd.
solutions.answer: If x is an odd integer, then x² − 4x + 6 is odd.
why: We begin with the condition that must be proved.
By the definition of an odd integer, it is one more than twice an integer.
Substitution replaces x with its odd-integer form.
Expanding the square and distributing −4 gives like terms to combine.
Combining like terms simplifies the expression.
Factoring out 2 shows the expression is twice an integer plus 1.
This matches the definition of an odd integer because the bracket is an integer.

solutions.question: Prove the following statements: If x is an even integer then show that x² + 2x + 4 is even.
steps: Let x be an even integer.
Then x = 2k for some integer k.
Since 2k² + 2k + 2 is an integer, x² + 2x + 4 is even.
solutions.answer: If x is an even integer, then x² + 2x + 4 is even.
why: We begin by assuming the condition in the statement.
By the definition of an even integer, it is twice an integer.
Substitution expresses the polynomial using the integer k.
Expanding and simplifying prepares the expression for factoring out 2.

explain.title: Negation
explain.body: If p is any statement, its negation is denoted by ~p, read ‘not p’. If p is true, ~p is false; if p is false, ~p is true.

explain.title: Conjunction
explain.body: The conjunction of two statements p and q is symbolically written as p ∧ q (p and q). A conjunction is considered to be true only if both statements are true.

explain.title: Disjunction
explain.body: The disjunction of p and q is symbolically written as p ∨ q (p or q). The disjunction p ∨ q is considered to be true when at least one of the statements is true. It is false when both of them are false.

explain.title: Conditional
explain.body: A compound statement of the form if p then q (p → q) also written as p implies q is called a conditional or an implication. p is called the antecedent or hypothesis and q is called the consequent or the conclusion. A conditional is regarded as false only when the antecedent is true and the consequent is false.

explain.title: Biconditional and related conditionals
explain.body: The statement p → q ∧ q → p is shortly written as p ↔ q and is called the biconditional or equivalence. It is read p iff q (iff stands for “if and only if”). For p → q, q → p is the converse, ~p → ~q is the inverse, and ~q → ~p is the contrapositive.

mistakes: Writing the converse when the question asks for the contrapositive: the contrapositive both swaps and negates the two parts.
Forgetting that the negation of ~p is p.
Marking p → q false whenever q is false. It is false only when p is true and q is false.
Treating p ∨ q as true only when both statements are true; that is the condition for a conjunction, not a disjunction.
Leaving out one of the four p, q combinations in a truth table.
Evaluating the final truth-table column before completing the inner operations.

recap.question: When is the conditional p → q false?
recap.answer: A conditional p → q is false only when p is true and q is false.

explain.title: What a proof does
explain.body: In mathematics, proofs provides the evidence that a statement is correct, demonstrating a logical sequence of steps that lead to the final conclusion. Each step should follow from a definition, a known fact, or a valid calculation.

explain.title: Use definitions to prove number statements

explain.title: Proving two sets are equal

explain.title: A proof needs a justified conclusion

explain.title: Theorem
explain.body: A theorem is a mathematical statement that has been proved true based on previously known facts. For example, the sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is 360 degrees.

explain.title: Conjecture
explain.body: A conjecture is a mathematical statement or hypothesis that is believed to be true based on observations but has not yet been proved. If it is proved true, it becomes a theorem; if it is disproved, it is false. The Goldbach Conjecture says every even integer greater than 2 is a sum of two prime numbers.

explain.title: Axiom
explain.body: An axiom is a mathematical statement that we believe to be true without any evidence or requiring any proof. In other words, these statements are basic facts that form the starting point for further ideas and are based on everyday experiences. Moreover, there is no evidence contradicting these statements. For example, through a given point, infinitely many lines can pass.

explain.title: Postulate
explain.body: Axioms are sometimes referred to as postulates. Both Axioms and Postulates describe statements that are accepted as true without requiring proof. However, postulates are associated explicitly with geometry, while axioms can pertain to broader mathematical contexts.

mistakes: Do not call a statement a theorem just because examples seem to support it; a theorem requires a proof.

explain.title: What deductive reasoning means
explain.body: Deductive reasoning draws a conclusion from premises believed to be true. If the premises are true, the conclusion must also be true. For example, if all human beings need to breathe to live and Ahmad is a human, we conclude that Ahmad also needs to breathe to live.

explain.title: Deductive proof in algebra
explain.body: Deductive proof in an algebraic expression is a technique to show the validity of a mathematical statement through logical reasoning based on known rules, theorems, axioms, or previously proven statements. Each line of a proof should follow from a valid rule or an earlier line.

explain.title: How to prove an identity
explain.body: Start with one side, usually the L.H.S. Expand or simplify it by valid steps until it matches the R.H.S. A proof is complete when you show L.H.S. = R.H.S. and state that the result is hence proved.

explain.title: Justifying steps
explain.body: When asked to justify each step, name the rule that allows the change. For instance, division by a number can be written as multiplication by its reciprocal, and factors common to numerator and denominator can be cancelled when they are non-zero.

mistakes: Starting with the R.H.S. and changing both sides at once makes it harder to show that the identity follows logically.
Skipping algebraic steps or giving an incorrect reason can lose method marks even if the final answer is right.

In an odd/even proof, do not just say the result looks odd or even. Show it as 2k + 1 or 2k, where the remaining expression is an integer.

solutions.question: Write the truth table of the following: ~(p ∨ q) ∨ (~q)
steps: Let the possible truth-value pairs for (p, q) be (T, T), (T, F), (F, T), and (F, F).
For (T, T): p ∨ q = T, ~(p ∨ q) = F, and ~q = F; hence ~(p ∨ q) ∨ (~q) = F.
For (T, F): p ∨ q = T, ~(p ∨ q) = F, and ~q = T; hence ~(p ∨ q) ∨ (~q) = T.
For (F, T): p ∨ q = T, ~(p ∨ q) = F, and ~q = F; hence ~(p ∨ q) ∨ (~q) = F.
For (F, F): p ∨ q = F, ~(p ∨ q) = T, and ~q = T; hence ~(p ∨ q) ∨ (~q) = T.

Truth table (rows are in the order (T, T), (T, F), (F, T), (F, F)): | p | q | p ∨ q | ~(p ∨ q) | ~q | ~(p ∨ q) ∨ (~q) |; | T | T | T | F | F | F |; | T | F | T | F | T | T |; | F | T | T | F | F | F |; | F | F | F | T | T | T |
solutions.answer: The truth values of ~(p ∨ q) ∨ (~q), in the order (T, T), (T, F), (F, T), (F, F), are F, T, F, T.
why: Two propositions have four possible truth-value pairs, which form the table rows.
For this row, disjunction is true if either input is true, then negation and disjunction give the result.
For this row, negating false gives true, so the final disjunction is true.
For this row, both negated parts are false, so their disjunction is false.
For this row, both negated parts are true, so their disjunction is true.
The table collects the values found for every possible input pair.

explain.title: What similar figures mean
explain.body: Your textbook defines similar figures as having the same shape but not necessarily the same size. Two polygons are similar if their corresponding angles are equal and the corresponding sides are proportional (i.e., the ratios of the lengths of corresponding sides are equal). The symbol for similarity is '~'.

explain.title: How to compare sides
explain.body: Match sides that connect corresponding vertices, then write their ratios in the same order. If the ratios are equal, the corresponding sides are proportional. For instance, 6/10.5 = 9/15.75 = 12/21 = 4/7.

explain.title: Ways to identify similar triangles
explain.body: The textbook shows that triangles are similar when two pairs of corresponding angles are equal, when the ratio of two corresponding sides and their included angle are equal, or when all ratios of corresponding sides are equal.

explain.title: Using similarity to find a length
explain.body: Once you know the triangles are similar, write a proportion using corresponding sides. Keep each pair in the same order, substitute the known lengths, and solve for the unknown.

mistakes: Pairing sides in the wrong order instead of matching corresponding vertices.
Checking only one pair of side ratios and claiming all corresponding sides are proportional.
Saying polygons are similar because their angles match without checking that their corresponding sides are proportional.
Reversing one ratio while writing a proportion.
Leaving off units from a length answer or rounding too early.

explain.title: Square the length ratio
explain.body: For similar figures, the ratio of their areas is the square of the ratio of any two corresponding lengths: A₁/A₂ = (ℓ₁/ℓ₂)². For example, lengths in the ratio 3:4 give areas in the ratio 9:16.

explain.title: Use the matching parts in order
explain.body: Keep the smaller figure's measurements together and the larger figure's measurements together. If the length ratio is 10:6, write the area ratio in that same order as A₁/A₂ = (10/6)².

explain.title: Find a missing length or a remaining area

explain.title: Similar solids
explain.body: Two solids are said to be similar if they have same shape but possibly different sizes. Their corresponding lengths are proportional.

explain.title: Volume ratio
explain.body: Hence the ratio of the volume of any two similar solids is equal to the cube of the ratio of any two corresponding lengths of the solids. In symbols, V₁/V₂ = (ℓ₁/ℓ₂)³.

explain.title: Scale factor
explain.body: Since each length is k times of the other, we take ℓ₁/ℓ₂ = k, then V₁/V₂ = k³. i.e., Volume V₁ is k³ times the volume V₂ and k is called scale factor.

explain.title: Mass and area ratios
explain.body: Since mass of a substance is proportional to its volume, the ratio of the mass of two similar solids is equal of to the ratio of their volumes. Use w₁/w₂ = (ℓ₁/ℓ₂)³ for masses. For surface areas, square the corresponding length ratio.

explain.title: Regular polygons and their angles
explain.body: A regular polygon has all sides and all angles equal. For a polygon with n sides, the sum of its interior angles is (n − 2) × 180°. In a regular polygon, divide this sum by n to get each interior angle. The exterior angles of any polygon add to 360°, so each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 360°/n. At each vertex, an interior angle and its exterior angle add to 180°.

explain.title: Diagonals and symmetry
explain.body: The total number of diagonals in a regular polygon with n sides is n(n − 3)/2. A regular n-sided polygon has rotational symmetry and reflexive symmetry both of order n. It has n lines of symmetry, and a rotation of 360°/n makes it look the same.

explain.title: Triangle properties
explain.body: A triangle's interior angles add to 180°. In an equilateral triangle, all sides are equal and each angle is 60°. In an isosceles triangle, two sides and the angles opposite those equal sides are equal. An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.

explain.title: Parallelograms and related shapes
explain.body: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel and equal in length and opposite angles are equal. Its adjacent angles are supplementary, and its diagonals bisect each other. A rectangle has all angles 90° and equal diagonals. A rhombus has all sides equal and diagonals that bisect each other at right angles. A square has all sides equal, all angles 90°, and diagonals that are equal and bisect each other at right angles.

explain.title: Tessellations and applications
explain.body: A tessellation is a pattern of shapes that fit together perfectly, without any gaps or overlaps, covering a plane. Equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons can tessellate on their own because their angles fit around a point to make 360°. Polygon area and angle properties also help solve problems about floors, walls, windows and other designs.

mistakes: Do not use (n − 2) × 180° as the measure of each interior angle; it gives the sum. Divide by n for each angle of a regular polygon.
Do not confuse an interior angle with an exterior angle: each regular exterior angle is 360°/n.
Do not assume the sloping side of a parallelogram is its height; the height must be perpendicular to the base.
Remember that adjacent angles in a parallelogram add to 180°, while opposite angles are equal.
For area and coverage questions, use square units for area and round a required number of tiles, gallons or litres up when a fraction remains.
Do not claim that regular pentagons tessellate on their own; the angles meeting at a point must add to 360°.

explain.title: What similarity tells you
explain.body: Similar polygons have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. Their shapes match, even if their sizes differ.

explain.title: Areas use the square
explain.body: If corresponding lengths are in the ratio a:b, the areas are in the ratio a²:b². This rule works for similar polygons and for surface areas of similar solids.

explain.title: Volumes and capacities use the cube

explain.title: Regular polygon angles
explain.body: A regular polygon's exterior angles add to 360°. So its number of sides is 360° divided by one exterior angle. An interior angle and its exterior angle add to 180°.

definitions.text: Three or more than three-sided closed figure is called polygon.
Similar figures have same shape but not necessarily of same size.

Two polygons are similar if their corresponding angles are equal and the corresponding sides are proportional (i.e., the ratios of the lengths of corresponding sides are equal). This means that if two polygons are similar, one is a scaled version of the other.
Proportionality of sides means one side is k times of its corresponding side.

If two angles in one triangle are congruent to two corresponding angles in another triangle, the third angle in each triangle must be congruent. Since the angles are the same, the triangles are similar. Similarity symbol is ‘~’.
If the ratio of two corresponding sides and their included angle are equal, then the triangles are similar.
If the ratio of all the corresponding sides are equal, then the triangles are similar.
Hence the ratio of the areas of any two similar figures is equal to the square of the ratio of any two corresponding lengths of the figures.
Since each length is k times of the other, we take ℓ₁/ℓ₂ = k, then A₁/A₂ = k². i.e. Area A₁ is k² times the area A₂. k is called scale factor.

Two solids are said to be similar if they have same shape but possibly different sizes. Two solids are similar if lengths of the corresponding sides are proportional i.e., the ratio of the corresponding lengths are equal.
Hence the ratio of the volume of any two similar solids is equal to the cube of the ratio of any two corresponding lengths of the solids.
Since mass of a substance is proportional to its volume, the ratio of the mass of two similar solids is equal of to the ratio of their volumes.

fullMarks: Start a similarity proof by naming the two figures and matching their corresponding vertices in the correct order, such as ΔABC ~ ΔDEF.
For a triangle similarity proof, show the matching angles or write all three corresponding side ratios and show that they are equal.
Keep the order of corresponding figures consistent in every ratio; do not compare a side with a non-corresponding side.
For area questions, write A₁/A₂ = (ℓ₁/ℓ₂)² before substituting values. For volume questions, write V₁/V₂ = (ℓ₁/ℓ₂)³.
If an area ratio is given and a length is required, take the square root of the area ratio. If a volume ratio is given and a length is required, take the cube root.
Show the proportion, substitution and rearrangement as separate steps, then write the final answer clearly.
Include the correct units in the final answer: cm² or m² for area, and cm³ or m³ for volume.
mistakes: Using the length ratio directly as the area ratio. Fix: square the corresponding-length ratio.
Using the square of the length ratio for volumes. Fix: cube the corresponding-length ratio.
Reversing one ratio but not the others. Fix: keep the same figure first in every numerator and the other figure in every denominator.
Taking a square root when finding a length from a volume ratio. Fix: take the cube root for volumes.
Matching sides in the wrong order when writing a triangle similarity statement. Fix: list the corresponding vertices in the same order before forming ratios.
Leaving off square or cubic units. Fix: write units such as cm² for area and cm³ for volume in the final answer.

explain.title: A function pairs inputs and outputs
explain.body: In y = f(x), x is the independent variable (input) and y is the dependent variable (output). A function can be shown as an equation, graph, table, or verbal description.

explain.title: Different functions have different graph shapes
explain.body: A linear function makes a straight line. A quadratic function makes a parabola: it opens upward when a > 0 and downward when a < 0. A cubic graph is a curve that can have at most two turning points.

explain.title: Reciprocal and exponential graphs
explain.body: A reciprocal function has the form y = a/x, with x ≠ 0. Its graph may approach asymptotes, which are lines that a graph approaches but never touches. An exponential function has the form y = kaˣ, where a > 1; y = 2ˣ is an increasing growth curve.

explain.title: Plot by making a table
explain.body: Choose several x-values, calculate y for each one, and plot the resulting points. Join the points with a straight line or a smooth curve that matches the type of function.

mistakes: Copying a sign incorrectly when substituting a negative x-value, especially when squaring or cubing.
Drawing a quadratic graph as a straight line instead of a parabola.
Joining plotted points with sharp corners instead of a smooth curve.
Forgetting that x cannot be zero in y = a/x, or plotting a point where a reciprocal function is undefined.
Drawing a reciprocal graph so that it touches an asymptote.
Leaving out labels, axes, intercepts, or the stated interval when sketching a graph.

explain.title: Exponential growth and decay
explain.body: In exponential growth, the graph starts slowly but accelerates rapidly as time progresses. In exponential decay, the graph starts high and decreases sharply before levelling off.

explain.title: Make a table before graphing
explain.body: Choose several values of time or another input, substitute them into the function, and record the outputs. Plot the ordered pairs and join them with a smooth curve when the relationship is exponential.

explain.title: Gradient at a point
explain.body: The gradient or slope of a graph at any point is equal to the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that point. Remember that a tangent is a line that just touches a curve only at one point (and doesn’t cross it).

explain.title: Real-life graphs
explain.body: A straight salary graph can show the starting salary and yearly increase. For cost and revenue, the point where the graphs meet is the break-even point; revenue minus cost gives profit.

mistakes: Using a year such as 2020 directly as t instead of measuring t from the starting year. In Example 12, 2020 corresponds to t = 10.
Plotting too few points when a graph is being used to estimate values between or across the given interval.
Reversing the gradient formula: use change in y divided by change in x.
For a tangent gradient, choosing two points on the curve instead of two points on the tangent line.
Finding break-even by subtracting cost from revenue without first setting R(x) = C(x).
For profit, forgetting to subtract cost from revenue or forgetting the fixed-cost term in the function.
Giving a numerical answer without its units, such as bags, persons, years, or rupees.

explain.title: Straight-line graphs
explain.body: A linear function such as y = 5x + 3 has a straight-line graph. In y = mx + c, m is the slope and c is the y-intercept. The equation x = 5 gives a vertical line parallel to the y-axis.

explain.title: Quadratic graphs
explain.body: A function with x² has a parabola as its graph. If the coefficient of x² is positive, the parabola opens upward; if it is negative, it opens downward.

explain.title: Cubic graphs
explain.body: A function with x³ is cubic. To find where its graph meets the x-axis, set y = 0 and solve the resulting equation.

explain.title: Exponential graphs
explain.body: In an exponential function, the variable is in the exponent, as in y = 5^x. A base greater than 1 gives growth as x increases; a base between 0 and 1 gives decay.

explain.title: Reciprocal graphs and plotting
explain.body: In a reciprocal function such as y = 2/x, x cannot be zero. Make a table of input-output values, plot the points, and sketch the separate branches without joining them across x = 0.

explain.title: Using graphs in applications
explain.body: A graph can show how quantities such as sales, cost, revenue, supply, or demand change. The break-even point is where cost and revenue are equal, so it is the intersection of their graphs.

definitions.text: A linear function is a mathematical expression that represents a straight-line relationship between two variables. Its general form is f(x) = mx + c, where “m” is the slope or gradient of the line, indicating how steep it is and “c” is the y-intercept (the point where the line crosses the y-axis). It can also be written as y = mx + c.

A quadratic function is a type of polynomial function that involves x² term. Its general form is:
y = ax² + bx + c
Where a, b, c are constants and a ≠ 0.

The graph of a quadratic function is always a parabola.
• If a > 0, then the parabola opens upward like “∪”.
• If a < 0, then the parabola opens downward like “∩”.

A cubic function is a type of polynomial function of degree 3. Its standard form is:
y = ax³ + bx² + cx + d
Where a, b, c, d are constants and a ≠ 0.

A reciprocal function is a function of the form:
y = a/x
Where a is any real number and x ≠ 0.
An asymptote is a line that a graph approaches but never touches.

An exponential function is a mathematical function of the form:
y = ka^x
Where a, k are constants, x is variable and a > 1.

explain.body: With two sides and an acute angle opposite one of them, the arc may meet the ray twice, touch it once, or not meet it. In Example 5, EF greater than 3 cm gives two triangles, EF equal to 3 cm gives one, and EF less than 3 cm gives none.

mistakes: Putting the included angle at the wrong endpoint or drawing it on the wrong side of the given line segment.
Using the wrong compass centre or radius, so the side lengths are not correct.
Joining the wrong intersection point or forgetting to label the vertices.
Assuming an acute-angle construction always gives two triangles; check whether the arc intersects, touches or misses the ray.
Ignoring the Triangle Inequality Theorem when deciding whether three given lengths can form a triangle.

solutions.question: Construct a triangle of sides 5.3 cm, 5.9 cm and 6.2 cm.
steps: (i) Draw a line segment AB of length 5.3cm long.
(ii) Using a pair of compasses, draw two arcs with centres at points A and B of radii 5.9 cm and 6.2 cm respectively.
(iii) These two arcs intersect each other at point C.
(iv) Join A and B with C.
Hence, ΔABC is the required triangle.
[Figure: Triangle ABC with AB labelled 5.3 cm, AC labelled 5.9 cm and BC labelled 6.2 cm.]

solutions.question: Construct a triangle BCD in which measures of two sides are 5.5 cm and 4.2 cm and measure of their included angle is 60°.
steps: (i) Draw a line segment BC of length 5.5cm.
(ii) Draw an angle 60° at point B using a pair of compasses and draw a ray BX through this angle.
(iii) Draw an arc of radius 4.2 cm with centre at point B intersecting BX at point D.
Hence, ΔBCD is the required triangle.
[Figure: Triangle BCD with BC labelled 5.5 cm, BD labelled 4.2 cm, angle CBD labelled 60°, and ray BX extending through D.]

solutions.question: Draw a triangle CDE when m D̅E̅ = 4.3 cm, m∠D = 30° and m∠E = 120°.
steps: (ii) Draw angles 30° and 120° at points D and E respectively using a pair of compasses and draw two rays through these angles from D and E.
(iii) These two rays intersect each other at point C.
Hence, ΔCDE is the required triangle.
[Figure: Triangle CDE with base DE labelled 4.3cm, angles 30° at D and 120° at E, and rays from D and E intersecting at C.]

solutions.question: Construct a triangle DEF when m D̅E̅ = 6 cm, m∠D = 110° and m E̅F̅ = 9 cm.
steps: (ii) Construct m∠D = 110° using protractor and draw D⃗X⃗ through this angle.
(iii) Draw an arc of radius 9 cm with centre at point E intersecting D⃗X⃗ at point F.
Hence, ΔDEF is the required triangle
(Figure: Triangle DEF with DE labelled 6 cm, EF labelled 9 cm, angle D labelled 110°, and ray DX extending beyond F to X.)
If the given angle opposite to the given side is obtuse, only one triangle is possible.
why: This heading introduces the construction procedure.
The known side provides a fixed base for locating the remaining vertex.
The angle ray fixes the direction from D in which F must lie.
The arc marks points exactly 9 cm from E, so its intersection gives F.
Joining E to F completes the triangle and uses the required side length.
This confirms the constructed triangle has the specified measurements.

An obtuse opposite angle restricts the possible intersection to at most one point.

solutions.question: Construct triangles DEF and DEF′ when m D̅E̅ = 6 cm, m∠D = 30° and m E̅F̅ = 3.6 cm
steps: (ii) Construct an angle 30° at point D using a pair of compasses and draw D→X through this angle.
(iii) Draw an arc of radius 3.6 cm with centre at point E.
(iv) This arc intersects D→X at two points F and F′.
(v) Join F and F′ with E.
We get two triangles DEF and DEF′.
This is known as ambiguous case.
[Figure: Two triangles DEF and DEF′ constructed on DE = 6 cm and a 30° angle at D, with EF and EF′ = 3.6 cm.]

modules.title: 11.2 Perpendicular Bisectors and Medians of a Triangle

bookReference.text: Your textbook, Unit 11, section 11.2, pages 204–205

examTips: A board question may ask you to state the definitions of a perpendicular bisector, median, circumcentre, or centroid. Use the precise defining features: equal halves and 90° for a perpendicular bisector; vertex and opposite-side midpoint for a median.
For a construction question, show the compass arcs and the lines drawn through their intersections. Mark the midpoints and label the constructed lines and concurrency points clearly.
When asked to find or identify the concurrency points, name the perpendicular-bisector point O as the circumcentre and the median point O′ as the centroid.
Keep the two constructions distinct: the perpendicular bisectors are made using arcs from the endpoints of each side; the medians are made by joining vertices to opposite-side midpoints.

hints: Begin by drawing triangle GEF using the three given side lengths.
For each side, construct its perpendicular bisector with equal-radius arcs from the endpoints; then join each vertex to the opposite midpoint.
yourTurn.question: Draw perpendicular bisector of the triangle EFG with mE̅F̅ = 5cm, mF̅G̅ = 2.5cm and mE̅G̅ = 4.3 cm. Find the medians.
solution: Draw △GEF as explained in the previous examples.
Draw two arcs above and below E̅F̅ with more than half of mE̅F̅ with centre at E.
Draw two arcs above and below E̅F̅ with radius more than half of mE̅F̅ with centre at F.
Draw a line through the points of intersection of the arcs in steps (ii) and (iii), to get the perpendicular bisector of EF at A.
Repeat to draw the perpendicular bisectors of FG and EG at B and C respectively.
Join G to opposite midpoint A to get median GA; join F to opposite midpoint C to get median FC; join E to opposite midpoint B to get median EB.
The perpendicular bisectors meet at O (the circumcentre), and the medians meet at O′ (the centroid).
yourTurn.answer: The medians are GA, FC and EB; the perpendicular bisectors meet at O and the medians meet at O′.

hints: Recall which lines meet at each named point.
The perpendicular bisectors meet at one named centre; the medians meet at the other.
yourTurn.question: What are the points of concurrency of the perpendicular bisectors and the medians of a triangle called?
solution: The point of concurrency of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle is called circumcentre.
The point of concurrency of the medians of a triangle is called centroid of the triangle.
yourTurn.answer: The perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre; the medians meet at the centroid.

example.answer: The medians are GA, FC and EB. The perpendicular bisectors are concurrent at O (the circumcentre), and the medians are concurrent at O′ (the centroid).

explain.title: Perpendicular bisector
explain.body: A perpendicular bisector is a line that intersects a line segment at right angle and dividing it into two equal parts. In other words, it intersects the line segment at its midpoint and forms right angles (90°) with it.

explain.title: Median
explain.body: A median of a triangle is a line segment that joins a vertex to the midpoint of the side that is opposite to that vertex.

explain.title: Point of concurrency
explain.body: A point of concurrency is the single point where three or more lines, rays or line segments intersect or meet in a geometric figure. This concept is commonly used in triangles, where several important types of points of concurrency exist.

explain.title: Two special points in a triangle
explain.body: The point of concurrency of perpendicular bisector of the sides of a triangle is called circumcentre. The point of concurrency of the medians of a triangle is called centroid of the triangle.

mistakes: Drawing a perpendicular bisector that does not meet the side at 90° or does not pass through its midpoint.
Using unequal compass radii from the two endpoints when constructing the perpendicular bisector.
Calling a line from a vertex to an arbitrary point on the opposite side a median; it must reach the midpoint.
Mixing up the names: perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre, while medians meet at the centroid.
Leaving construction arcs, midpoint labels, or the concurrency points unclear in a construction answer.

recap.question: When one side and two angles are given, what marks the third vertex?
recap.answer: The two rays meet at the third vertex.

recap.question: Total parts of a triangle are:

solutions.question: Draw perpendicular bisector of the triangle EFG with mE̅F̅ = 5cm, mF̅G̅ = 2.5cm and mE̅G̅ = 4.3 cm. Find the medians.
steps: First we draw perpendicular bisectors and then medians.
i. Draw △GEF as explained in the previous examples.
ii. Draw two arcs above and below E̅F̅ with more than half of mE̅F̅ with centre at E.
iii. Draw two arcs above and below E̅F̅ with radius more than half of mE̅F̅ with centre at F.
iv. Draw a line through the points of intersection of the arcs in steps (ii) and (iii), we get the perpendicular bisector ↔LL′ of the side EF at A.
v. Draw two more perpendicular bisectors ↔MM′ and ↔NN′ of the sides FG and EG at B and C respectively.
(Figure: Triangle EFG with perpendicular bisectors and medians drawn, showing points A, B, C, O and O′.)
vi. Join the point G with opposite midpoint A so GA is the median.
vii. Join the point F with opposite midpoint C, we get median FC and join point E with opposite midpoint B, we get median EB.
Hence, we see that the perpendicular bisector LL′, MM′ and NN′ are concurrent at point O or A and the medians GA, EB and FC are concurrent at point O′.
Circumcentre: The point of concurrency of perpendicular bisector of the sides of a triangle is called circumcentre.
Centroid: The point of concurrency of the medians of a triangle is called centroid of the triangle.
why: Perpendicular bisectors locate the circumcentre, while medians locate the centroid.

This definition names where all three medians meet.

explain.title: What an angle bisector does
explain.body: An angle bisector of a triangle is a line or ray that divides an angle into two equal parts, creating two smaller angles that are congruent (each having half the measure of the original angle).

explain.title: Constructing an angle bisector
explain.body: Use an arc centred at the angle’s vertex to mark both sides. Then draw arcs from those two marks and draw a ray from the vertex through the arcs’ intersection.

explain.title: The incentre
explain.body: The angle bisectors of a triangle are concurrent: they meet at one point. The point of concurrency of the angle bisectors of a triangle is called incentre of the triangle.

mistakes: Drawing the first arc from a point other than the angle’s vertex.
Using different radii for the two arcs from the side-intersection points.
Drawing the final ray from the wrong vertex or not through the arcs’ intersection.
Calling the common point a centroid or an orthocentre instead of an incentre.

recap.question: What is the name of the point where the medians of a triangle meet?
recap.answer: The circumcentre is where the perpendicular bisectors meet; the centroid is where the medians meet.

steps: We first construct triangle FGH, then draw its angle bisector.

(iii) Draw two arcs with centres at points A and B with suitable radius.
(iv) Draw a ray from F passing through the point of intersection of the arcs in step (iii). Which is the required angle bisector F→P of the angle F.
(Figure: Triangle FGH with angle bisectors F→P, G→Q and H→R meeting at O; points A, B, P, Q, R, X and labels 5.2 cm and 4.1 cm.)

We see that all the angle bisectors F→P, G→Q and H→R intersect at one point O, i.e., the angle bisectors of the triangle are concurrent.

explain.title: What is an altitude?
explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “Altitude is a ray drawn perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side of the triangle.” In other words, it starts at a triangle’s vertex and meets the opposite side at a right angle. The opposite side may need to be extended.

explain.title: Altitudes meet at one point
explain.body: There is one altitude from each of the three vertices. Your textbook states: “There are three altitudes of the triangle which meet at a single point i.e. the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent.” The common meeting point is called the orthocentre.

explain.title: Finding the orthocentre in a construction
explain.body: First construct the triangle from the measurements given. Then draw a perpendicular from each vertex to its opposite side or the extension of that side. The point where the perpendiculars meet is the orthocentre.

explain.title: The orthocentre
explain.body: Your textbook defines it as: “The point of concurrency of the altitudes of the triangle is called orthocentre of the triangle.” Label the common point clearly in your construction.

mistakes: Drawing a perpendicular from a vertex to a side that is not opposite that vertex.

Assuming an altitude must always fall on the side segment instead of allowing the side to be extended.

Failing to label the common intersection as the orthocentre.

solutions.question: Construct △ABC with the given measurements and verify that the perpendicular bisectors of the triangle are concurrent: m A̅B̅ = 5 cm, m B̅C̅ = 6 cm and m A̅C̅ = 7 cm.
steps: With centre A and radius 7 cm, draw an arc.
With centre B and radius 6 cm, draw an arc intersecting the first arc at C.
Join AC and BC to obtain △ABC.
With a compass, draw equal-radius arcs from A and B, above and below AB, and join the arc intersections to construct the perpendicular bisector of AB.
In the same way, construct the perpendicular bisectors of BC and AC.
Mark the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC as O.
Observe that the perpendicular bisector of AC also passes through O.
Thus, the perpendicular bisectors of △ABC are concurrent at O, and OA = OB = OC.
solutions.answer: The perpendicular bisectors of △ABC are concurrent at O, the circumcentre.
solutions.figure: △ABC with AB = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm and AC = 7 cm. The perpendicular bisectors meet at O, the circumcentre; OA = OB = OC.
why: The known side gives a fixed base for constructing the triangle.
A radius of 7 cm ensures C is 7 cm from A.
The second arc ensures C is also 6 cm from B.
Joining the sides completes the triangle with the required lengths.
Equal-radius arcs construct a line perpendicular to AB at its midpoint.
Repeating this construction gives the other two perpendicular bisectors.
Two constructed lines determine the point O to test.
The third bisector passing through O verifies concurrency.
Equal distances from O to all vertices confirm it is the circumcentre.

solutions.question: Construct △ABC with the given measurements and verify that the perpendicular bisectors of the triangle are concurrent: m A̅B̅ = 7.1 cm, m∠B = 135° and m B̅C̅ = 6.5 cm.
steps: At B, construct ∠ABX = 135° using a protractor.
On ray BX, mark C such that BC = 6.5 cm.
Join A to C to obtain △ABC.
Construct the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC using equal-radius compass arcs.
Construct the perpendicular bisector of AC and observe that it passes through O.
Thus, the perpendicular bisectors of △ABC are concurrent at O.
solutions.answer: The perpendicular bisectors of △ABC are concurrent at O, the circumcentre.
solutions.figure: △ABC with AB = 7.1 cm, ∠B = 135° and BC = 6.5 cm. Its perpendicular bisectors meet at O, the circumcentre.
why: The known side provides a fixed length for constructing the triangle.
The protractor sets the required direction of the next side from B.
Marking the given length places C correctly on the angle ray.
Joining A to C closes the triangle.
Compass arcs construct lines perpendicular to the sides at their midpoints.
The first two bisectors determine their meeting point O.
The third bisector tests whether all three meet at the same point.
A shared intersection confirms the perpendicular bisectors are concurrent.

solutions.question: Construct △LMN of the following measurements and verify that the medians of the triangle are concurrent: m L̅M̅ = 4.9 cm, m∠L = 51° and m∠M = 38°.
steps: At L, construct ∠MLX = 51° using a protractor.
At M, construct ∠LMY = 38° on the same side of LM.
Mark the intersection of rays LX and MY as N, and join LN and MN to obtain △LMN.
Construct the perpendicular bisectors of LM and mark their intersection with LM as its midpoint.
In the same way, construct the midpoints of MN and NL.
Join each vertex to the midpoint of its opposite side to draw the three medians.
Mark the intersection of two medians as G.
Observe that the third median also passes through G.
Thus, the medians of △LMN are concurrent at G, the centroid.
solutions.answer: The medians of △LMN are concurrent at G, the centroid.
solutions.figure: △LMN with LM = 4.9 cm, ∠L = 51° and ∠M = 38°. The medians meet at G, the centroid.
why: The known side provides a fixed base for the triangle.
The first angle fixes the direction of side LN.
The second angle fixes the direction of side MN on the same side of the base.
The rays locate N, and joining the sides completes the triangle.
A perpendicular bisector crosses a side at its midpoint, identifying the required locations.
Repeating the midpoint construction locates the remaining side midpoints.
A median is defined as a segment joining a vertex to the opposite midpoint.
Two medians determine their intersection point G.
The third median passing through G verifies concurrency.
The shared meeting point is the triangle’s centroid.

solutions.question: Construct △LMN of the following measurements and verify that the medians of the triangle are concurrent: m M̅N̅ = 4.8 cm, m∠N = 30° and m L̅M̅ = 8.1 cm.
steps: At N, construct ∠MNY = 30° using a protractor, on one side of MN.
With centre M and radius 8.1 cm, draw an arc cutting ray NY at L.
Construct the perpendicular bisectors of LM, MN and NL to mark the midpoints of these sides.
Join each vertex to the midpoint of its opposite side to draw the three medians.
Mark the intersection of two medians as G.
Observe that the third median also passes through G.
Thus, the medians of △LMN are concurrent at G, the centroid.
solutions.answer: The medians of △LMN are concurrent at G, the centroid.
solutions.figure: △LMN with MN = 4.8 cm, ∠N = 30° and LM = 8.1 cm. The medians meet at G, the centroid.
why: The known side provides a fixed base for constructing the triangle.
The angle ray fixes the direction from N for locating L.
The arc locates a point 8.1 cm from M on the required ray.
Joining the sides completes the triangle with the given measurements.
Perpendicular bisectors cross the sides at their midpoints.
Joining vertices to opposite midpoints constructs the medians.
Two medians determine the point G to check.
The third median passing through G verifies concurrency.
The shared meeting point is called the centroid.

solutions.question: Verify that the angle bisectors of △ABC are concurrent with the following measurement: m A̅B̅ = 4.5 cm, m∠A = 45° and m A̅C̅ = 5.3 cm.
steps: At A, construct ∠BAX = 45° using a protractor.
On ray AX, mark C such that AC = 5.3 cm.
Join B to C to obtain △ABC.
Construct the bisectors of ∠A and ∠B using compass arcs.
Construct the bisector of ∠C and observe that it also passes through I.
Thus, the angle bisectors of △ABC are concurrent at I, the incentre.
solutions.answer: The angle bisectors of △ABC are concurrent at I, the incentre.
solutions.figure: △ABC with AB = 4.5 cm, ∠A = 45° and AC = 5.3 cm. The three internal angle bisectors meet at I, the incentre.
why: The known side fixes the length of one triangle side.
The protractor sets the direction of AC from A.
Marking the length places C at the required distance from A.
Joining B to C closes the triangle.
Compass arcs construct angle bisectors by locating points equidistant from each angle’s sides.
Two bisectors determine their intersection I.
The third bisector passing through I verifies concurrency.
The common meeting point of the angle bisectors is the incentre.

solutions.question: Verify that the angle bisectors of △ABC are concurrent with the following measurement: m A̅B̅ = 6 cm, m∠A = 150° and m∠B = 60°.
steps: The sum of the given angles is ∠A + ∠B = 150° + 60° = 210°.
But the sum of the angles of a triangle is 180°.
Since 210° > 180°, △ABC cannot be constructed with the given measurements.
Therefore, the angle bisectors of such a triangle cannot be drawn or verified.
solutions.answer: No such triangle can be constructed because 150° + 60° > 180°.
solutions.figure: No triangle can be constructed: the given angles ∠A = 150° and ∠B = 60° have sum 210°, which is greater than 180°.
why: This adds the given angles to check whether they can belong to one triangle.
A triangle’s interior angles must total 180 degrees.
The given total exceeds the triangle-angle sum, so the measurements are impossible.
Without a valid triangle, its angle bisectors cannot be constructed or checked.

solutions.question: Given the measurements of △DEF : m D̅E̅ = 4.8 cm, m E̅F̅ = 4 cm and m∠E = 45°, draw altitudes of △DEF and find orthocentre.
steps: At E, construct ∠FEX = 45° using a protractor.
On ray EX, mark D such that ED = 4.8 cm.
Join D to F to obtain △DEF.
Through D, draw a line perpendicular to EF; this is an altitude of △DEF.
Through F, draw a line perpendicular to DE; this is another altitude.
Mark the intersection of these altitudes as H.
Through E, draw a line perpendicular to DF and observe that it passes through H.
Thus, the altitudes of △DEF are concurrent at H, the orthocentre.
solutions.answer: The orthocentre of △DEF is H, the point of concurrency of its altitudes.
solutions.figure: △DEF with DE = 4.8 cm, EF = 4 cm and ∠E = 45°. The altitudes meet at H, the orthocentre, inside the triangle.
why: A fixed side gives a straight starting edge for the triangle.
The angle rule fixes the direction of side ED from E.
A compass marks the required length ED accurately on the chosen ray.
Joining the remaining endpoints closes the triangle.
An altitude is perpendicular to the opposite side, so this gives one altitude.
This perpendicular is another altitude, drawn from a different vertex.
The crossing point identifies where the two altitudes meet.
The third altitude checks that all three altitudes pass through the same point.
The concurrency property defines their common intersection as the orthocentre.

solutions.question: Construct the following triangles and find whether there exists any ambiguous case: △BCD ; m B̅C̅ = 5 cm, m∠B = 62° and m C̅D̅ = 4.7 cm.
steps: At B, construct ∠CBX = 62° using a protractor, on one side of BC.
With centre C and radius 4.7 cm, draw an arc cutting ray BX at D₁ and D₂.
The two triangles △BCD₁ and △BCD₂ both satisfy BC = 5 cm, ∠B = 62° and CD = 4.7 cm.
Therefore, two different triangles can be constructed from the given measurements; this is an ambiguous case.
solutions.answer: There are two possible triangles, so the given measurements form an ambiguous case.
solutions.figure: With BC = 5 cm and ∠B = 62°, the circle centred at C with radius 4.7 cm cuts the ray from B in two points, D₁ and D₂. Hence two triangles, △BCD₁ and △BCD₂, are possible: this is an ambiguous case.
why: A known side provides the base for the construction.
The given angle fixes the direction in which D can lie.
The circle enforces CD = 4.7 cm, and its two crossings give possible positions for D.
Joining each possible position to C completes both candidate triangles.
Checking each candidate against the measurements shows both satisfy the given data.
Two valid triangles from the same measurements are exactly an ambiguous case.

solutions.question: Construct the following triangles and find whether there exists any ambiguous case: △KLM ; m L̅M̅ = 6 cm, m∠M = 42° and m L̅N̅ = 5 cm.
steps: In triangle KLM, N is not a named vertex, so the given length LN does not specify a side of that triangle.
The printed measurements therefore do not define a construction for triangle KLM.
A correction to the stated side or vertex is needed before the ambiguous-case construction can be determined.
solutions.answer: A triangle KLM cannot be constructed uniquely from the data as printed; LN is not a side of triangle KLM.
solutions.figure: No determinate triangle can be drawn from the measurements as printed.
solutions.note: Since N is not a vertex of triangle KLM, the length LN does not determine one of its sides.
why: A valid triangle measurement must refer to vertices or sides of that triangle.
Without a defined side LN, the given data cannot determine the construction.
Correcting the vertex or side makes it possible to test for ambiguity.

examTips: Construction questions may ask you to draw one or more loci and label their intersection; use the correct construction for each condition.
For a point at a fixed distance from a point, draw a circle with that point as centre and the given distance as radius.
For a point equidistant from two points, construct the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them; for a point equidistant from two intersecting lines, construct the angle bisector.
Marks are earned by drawing the correct loci, placing the required point at their intersection, and labelling it clearly.
For scale questions, convert the real distance to the drawing distance using the stated scale, then convert any measured drawing distance back to the real distance.

explain.title: What is a locus?
explain.body: A locus (plural loci) is a set of points that follow a given rule. It tells us where a point can be when it obeys a condition.

explain.title: Common loci in two dimensions
explain.body: The locus of a point whose distance is constant from a fixed point is called a circle. Points at a constant distance from a fixed line form two parallel lines. Points equidistant from two fixed points lie on their perpendicular bisector. Points equidistant from two intersecting lines lie on an angle bisector.

explain.title: Intersections of loci
explain.body: If two or more loci intersect at a point P, then P satisfies all given conditions of the loci. Draw each locus and mark the intersection that meets the question's location requirement.

explain.title: Using a scale
explain.body: In Example 12, the scale is 10 m = 1 cm. So 13 m is represented by 1.3 cm, and a drawing length of 1.3 cm represents 13 m in the field.

mistakes: Drawing a circle with the wrong centre or radius for a fixed-distance condition.
Using the angle bisector when the condition is equidistance from two points, or using the perpendicular bisector when the condition is equidistance from two lines.
Marking a point on only one locus instead of at the intersection of all required loci.
Forgetting to choose the intersection inside the given shape when the question specifies it.
Using the scale in the wrong direction or forgetting to write the real measurement with its units.

The two loci intersect at P inside the rectangle which is 2 cm from point A and equidistant from A and B.
(Figure: Rectangle ABCD with a circle centered at A and a perpendicular bisector of AB; their intersection P lies inside the rectangle.)
why: The four sides and right angles define the required rectangle.

The sketch helps show the loci and the required interior intersection.

why: The given equal sides and vertex angle determine the isosceles triangle.
A circle represents all points exactly 2 cm from E.
An angle bisector contains points equally distant from both sides, so its intersection with the circle gives X.
The diagram clarifies the triangle, measurements, and location of the two loci.

The perpendicular bisector gives points equally distant from L and M, while the angle bisector gives points equally distant from the sides.

examTips: Locus questions commonly ask you to construct or draw a set of points satisfying a distance condition.
For a fixed distance from one point, show the centre and draw the circle with the stated radius.
For equal distances from two points, construct the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
When a question gives two conditions, use both loci and mark the required intersection point or points clearly.
Use the stated lengths and label points and constructed loci neatly; an accurate construction and the correct final point both matter.

explain.title: Locus for equal distances from two points
explain.body: Your textbook says: “Draw the perpendicular bisector of XY which represents the locus of all points equidistant from X and Y.” So if a point must be equally far from two fixed points, construct the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.

explain.title: Locus for a fixed distance from one point
explain.body: If every point must be the same distance from one fixed point, the locus is a circle. The fixed point is the centre, and the required distance is the radius.

explain.title: Use more than one condition
explain.body: When a question gives two conditions, construct the locus for each condition. Any point satisfying both conditions lies where the two loci meet.

explain.title: Loci in real situations
explain.body: A place equally accessible to two water sources can be chosen on their perpendicular bisector. A safety boundary a fixed distance from a source can be shown by a circle.

mistakes: Drawing a circle when the condition is equal distance from two points; that condition needs a perpendicular bisector.
Using a perpendicular bisector when the condition is a fixed distance from just one point; that condition needs a circle.
Setting the compass to the wrong radius or measuring from the wrong centre.
Forgetting to mark the intersection when a question gives two conditions.
Leaving the constructed line or circle unlabeled, or drawing it inaccurately.
