solutions.answer: The required locus is the circle with centre A and radius 5 cm.
solutions.figure: The finished figure shows AB = 8.2 cm and a circle with centre A and radius 5 cm. The circle is the locus of points 5 cm from A.
why: The segment fixes the known distance between the two reference points.
A compass set to 5 cm transfers the required radius accurately.
A circle contains every point exactly 5 cm from its centre.

solutions.question: Construct a locus of point 2.2 cm from line segment CD of measure 5.7cm.
steps: At C and D, construct perpendiculars to CD on both sides of CD.
On each perpendicular, mark points 2.2 cm from CD.
Through the marked points, draw lines parallel to CD, joining the corresponding points on each side.
With centres C and D and radius 2.2 cm, draw the semicircular arcs at the ends to join the parallel portions.
solutions.answer: The required locus is the boundary formed by the two parallel portions and the semicircular ends, all at a distance of 2.2 cm from CD.
solutions.figure: The finished figure shows CD = 5.7 cm, two parallel line segments 2.2 cm from CD on opposite sides, and semicircular ends of radius 2.2 cm centred at C and D. Together, these form the locus of points 2.2 cm from the segment CD.
why: The segment provides the finite line whose distance locus is required.
Perpendiculars provide directions for marking the fixed distance from CD.
These marks set the required offset on both sides of the segment.
Parallel lines keep every point on each straight part 2.2 cm from CD.
The semicircles complete the locus around the segment’s endpoints.

solutions.question: Construct an angle ABC = 105°. Construct a locus of a point P which moves such that it is equidistant from ray BA and ray BC.
steps: Assume P is restricted to the inside of ∠ABC, as the book intends.
Draw ray BC and use a protractor at B to construct ray BA so that ∠ABC = 105°.
With B as centre and compass radius 3 cm, draw an arc cutting BA at D and BC at E.
With D and E as centres and the same compass radius 3 cm, draw arcs intersecting at P inside the angle.
Draw ray BP. It bisects the 105° angle, so each half is 52.5°.
solutions.answer: The required locus inside ∠ABC is the angle-bisector ray BP, with ∠ABP = ∠PBC = 52.5°.
solutions.figure: ∠ABC = 105° with internal angle-bisector ray BP; P lies on the locus equidistant from arms BA and BC.
solutions.note: The construction gives the internal locus, as intended; if points outside the angle are included, the external angle bisector is also a locus.
why: Restricting P to the angle interior selects the intended angle-bisector ray.
The protractor sets the required angle accurately at its vertex.
Equal-radius arcs mark matching distances along both arms of the angle.
Matching arcs locate a point equally distant from the two arms.
Joining the vertex to that point draws the angle bisector, which halves the angle.

solutions.question: Two points E and F are 5.4 cm apart. Construct a locus of a point P which moves such that it is equidistant from E and F.
steps: With centres E and F and equal radii greater than half of EF, draw arcs above and below EF to intersect at P and Q.
solutions.answer: The required locus is the perpendicular bisector of EF.
solutions.figure: The finished figure shows EF = 5.4 cm and its perpendicular bisector. Every point on this perpendicular bisector is equidistant from E and F.
why: The segment provides the two fixed points for the locus construction.
Equal-radius arcs locate points equally distant from E and F on both sides.
The line through those intersections is the perpendicular bisector, the locus equidistant from E and F.

solutions.question: The island has two main cities A and B 8 km apart. Kashif lives on the island exactly 6.8 km from city A and exactly 7.3 km from city B. Mark with a cross the points on the island where Kashif could live.

With centre B and radius 7.3 km, draw a circle.
Mark the two intersection points of the circles with crosses.
solutions.answer: There are two possible points where Kashif could live.
solutions.figure: The finished figure shows AB = 8 km, a circle centred at A with radius 6.8 km, and a circle centred at B with radius 7.3 km. The two intersection points are marked with crosses; either point is a possible location of Kashif's home.
why: The segment represents the cities at their given separation.
The first circle represents all island locations 6.8 km from A.
The second circle represents all locations 7.3 km from B.
Their intersections satisfy both distance conditions, so they are possible homes.

solutions.question: Construct a triangle CDE with mC̅D̅ = 7.6 cm, m∠D = 45° and mD̅E̅ = 5.9 cm. Draw the locus of all points which are: (a) equidistant from C and D
steps: At D, construct a 45° angle with DC as one arm and draw the ray for DE.
On this ray, mark E so that DE = 5.9 cm.
With centres C and D and equal radii greater than half of CD, draw arcs intersecting above and below CD.
Join the two arc-intersection points to draw the perpendicular bisector of CD.
solutions.answer: The required locus is the perpendicular bisector of CD.
solutions.figure: The finished figure shows △CDE with CD = 7.6 cm, ∠CDE = 45°, and DE = 5.9 cm. The perpendicular bisector of CD is drawn; every point on it is equidistant from C and D.
why: The known side gives a fixed base for constructing the triangle.
The angle fixes the direction of the unknown side DE.
Marking the length fixes the position of E on the ray.
Joining the remaining vertices completes the triangle.
Equal-radius arcs locate points equally distant from C and D.
The perpendicular bisector is the locus of points equidistant from C and D.

solutions.question: Construct a triangle CDE with mC̅D̅ = 7.6 cm, m∠D = 45° and mD̅E̅ = 5.9 cm. Draw the locus of all points which are: (b) equidistant from C̅D̅ and C̅E̅
steps: At D, construct a perpendicular ray to DC on the chosen side using compass arcs; bisect the 90° angle between DC and this perpendicular ray to obtain a 45° ray DE.
On ray DE, mark E so that DE=5.9 cm, then join C to E.
At C, draw an arc of any convenient radius cutting CD and CE at X and Y.
With the same radius, draw arcs centered at X and Y to meet at Z inside ∠DCE.
Draw ray CZ; its portion from C to side DE is the required internal angle-bisector locus.
solutions.answer: The required locus inside triangle CDE is the internal angle bisector of ∠DCE.
solutions.figure: Triangle CDE has CD=7.6 cm, DE=5.9 cm and ∠CDE=45°. The internal bisector of ∠DCE runs from C to side DE and shows the required locus within the triangle.
solutions.note: Assume the required locus is the internal angle bisector within the triangle, as the book intends.
why: A fixed side gives a reliable starting point for constructing the triangle.
A perpendicular makes a right angle, and bisecting it gives the required 45° angle.
Marking the given length fixes E’s position on the constructed ray.
The arc creates two points equally far from C on the two sides of the angle.
Equal-radius arcs locate a point equally distant from the angle’s sides.
Joining the vertex to that point gives the angle bisector, whose points are equidistant from the sides.

solutions.question: Construct a triangle CDE with mC̅D̅ = 7.6 cm, m∠D = 45° and mD̅E̅ = 5.9 cm. Draw the locus of all points which are: (c) mark the point X where the two loci intersect.
steps: Construct △CDE with CD = 7.6 cm, DE = 5.9 cm and ∠D = 45°.
Construct the perpendicular bisector of CD; this is the locus of points equidistant from C and D.
Construct both the internal and external angle bisectors of ∠DCE; these are the loci of points equidistant from CD and CE.
Mark X at the intersection of the perpendicular bisector of CD and the internal angle bisector of ∠DCE.
solutions.answer: Assuming the first locus is the perpendicular bisector of CD, X is its intersection with the internal angle bisector of ∠DCE.
solutions.figure: Assuming the omitted first locus is the set of points equidistant from C and D, the figure shows its perpendicular bisector intersecting the two angle-bisector lines of ∠DCE. Mark X at the intersection of the perpendicular bisector CD and the internal angle bisector; this intersection lies inside △CDE.
why: The given side lengths and angle determine the triangle needed for the loci.
The perpendicular bisector contains exactly the points equally distant from C and D.
Angle bisectors contain points equally distant from the two lines forming the angle.
Their intersection satisfies both distance conditions; the internal bisector gives a point inside the angle.

solutions.question: Construct a triangle LMN with mL̅M̅ = 7 cm, m∠L = 70° and m∠M = 45°. Find a point within the triangle LMN which is equidistant from L and M and 3 cm from L.
steps: At L, construct a 70° angle with LM as one arm and draw ray LN.
At M, construct a 45° angle with ML as one arm and draw ray MN to meet ray LN at N.
Construct the perpendicular bisector of LM; every point on it is equidistant from L and M.
With centre L and radius 3 cm, draw a circle.
The perpendicular bisector is 3.5 cm from L, since it passes through the midpoint of LM.
Since 3 cm is less than 3.5 cm, the circle does not intersect the perpendicular bisector.
solutions.figure: The completed construction shows △LMN, the perpendicular bisector of LM, and the circle with centre L and radius 3 cm. The circle does not meet the perpendicular bisector, so there is no required point.
why: The side length provides the base needed to construct the triangle.
The ray fixes one side’s direction at the required angle.
The second ray and its intersection determine the third vertex.
Joining the vertices shows the completed triangle.
The perpendicular bisector is the locus of points equally distant from the segment’s endpoints.
A circle represents all points exactly 3 cm from L.
The midpoint is 3.5 cm from L because LM is 7 cm and the midpoint halves it.
The two loci cannot intersect, so no point satisfying both conditions exists inside the triangle.

solutions.question: Construct a right angled triangle RST with mR̅S̅ = 6.8 cm, m∠S = 90° and mS̅T̅ = 7.5 cm. Find a point within the triangle RST which is equidistant from R̅S̅ and R̅T̅ and 4.5 cm from R.
steps: At S, construct a perpendicular to RS.
On this perpendicular, mark T so that ST = 7.5 cm.
Join R to T. Triangle RST is constructed.
Bisect ∠SRT and draw its internal angle bisector.
With R as centre and radius 4.5 cm, draw an arc cutting the angle bisector at P inside triangle RST.
solutions.figure: Right triangle RST is constructed. The internal angle bisector of ∠SRT meets the circle centred at R with radius 4.5 cm at a point P inside the triangle.
why: The given side length establishes the triangle’s base.
A perpendicular constructs the required right angle at S.
Marking the second side fixes the location of T.
The final side completes the triangle.
Angle-bisector points are equally distant from the two sides of the angle.
The arc represents points 4.5 cm from R, so its intersection gives the required point.

solutions.question: Construct a rectangle UVWX with mU̅V̅ = 7.2 cm and mV̅W̅ = 5.6 cm. Draw the locus of points at a distance of 2 cm from U̅V̅ and 3.5 cm from W.
steps: At V, construct a perpendicular to UV and mark W on it so that VW = 5.6 cm.
Through U, construct a perpendicular to UV and mark X so that UX = 5.6 cm.
Join W to X to complete rectangle UVWX.
Draw the two line segments parallel to UV at a perpendicular distance of 2 cm from UV, one on each side of UV.
With centres U and V and radius 2 cm, draw the semicircular end arcs joining the parallel segments. These arcs and segments form the complete locus 2 cm from segment UV.
With centre W and radius 3.5 cm, draw a circle.
The shortest distance from W to segment UV is 5.6 cm, so the nearest point of the 2 cm locus is 5.6 − 2 = 3.6 cm from W.
Since 3.5 cm is less than 3.6 cm, the circle does not meet the 2 cm locus.
solutions.answer: The two loci do not intersect.
solutions.figure: The completed figure shows rectangle UVWX, the complete locus 2 cm from segment UV (the two parallel segments and the semicircular end arcs), and the circle centred at W with radius 3.5 cm. The two loci do not intersect.
why: The given side length starts the rectangle construction.
A perpendicular gives the right angle needed at V.
A matching perpendicular side gives the rectangle’s other corner.
Joining opposite corners completes the rectangle.
Parallel lines at perpendicular distance 2 cm give the straight portions of the locus.
The end arcs complete the set of points 2 cm from the whole segment UV.
A circle represents all points exactly 3.5 cm from W.
The nearest point of the distance-2 locus is 2 cm from UV, leaving 3.6 cm to W.
Because the circle’s radius is smaller than this minimum distance, the loci do not intersect.

solutions.question: Imagine two cell towers located at points A and B on a coordinate plane. The GPS-enabled device, positioned somewhere on the plane, receives signals from both towers. To ensure accurate navigation, the device is placed equidistant from both towers to estimate its position. Draw this locus of navigation.
steps: Mark the positions of the two towers as A and B.
With A and B as centres and the same radius greater than half of AB, draw arcs above and below AB so that the arcs intersect.
Join the two points where the arcs intersect.
solutions.answer: The perpendicular bisector of AB is the locus of points equidistant from A and B.
solutions.figure: The locus is the straight line perpendicular to AB through its midpoint, called the perpendicular bisector of AB.
why: Naming the tower positions identifies the two fixed points used to construct the locus.
Equal-radius arcs locate points equally distant from A and B.
The line through the arc intersections is the perpendicular bisector, containing all points equally distant from the towers.

solutions.question: Epidemiologists use loci to determine infection zones, especially for contagious diseases, to predict the spread and take containment measures. In the case of a disease outbreak, authorities might determine a quarantine zone within 10 km of the infection source. Draw the locus of all points 10 km from the source defining the quarantine area to monitor and control the disease's spread.
steps: Mark the infection source as O.
Using a suitable scale, set the compass to represent 10 km.
With O as centre, draw a circle of radius 10 km.
solutions.answer: The locus of points 10 km from the source is the circle centred at the source with radius 10 km.
solutions.figure: A circle with centre at the infection source and radius 10 km shows the boundary of the quarantine zone; the area inside it is within 10 km of the source.
why: A labelled centre identifies the source of the distance measurements.
The scale converts the real distance into a usable drawing measurement.
A circle contains exactly the points 10 km from its centre.

solutions.question: There is a treasure buried somewhere on the island. The treasure is 24 kilometres from A and equidistant from B and C. Using a scale of 1cm to represent 10 km, find where the treasure could be buried.
steps: Using the given scale, represent 24 km by 2.4 cm.
With A as centre and radius 2.4 cm, draw a circle.
Construct the perpendicular bisector of BC.
Mark the point(s) where the circle and the perpendicular bisector intersect.
solutions.answer: The treasure could be buried at the intersection point(s) of the circle centred at A with radius 2.4 cm and the perpendicular bisector of BC.
solutions.figure: The possible treasure locations are the intersection point(s) of the circle centred at A with radius 2.4 cm and the perpendicular bisector of BC.
why: The scale converts the treasure’s real distance into a drawing length.
A circle represents every location 2.4 cm from A.
The perpendicular bisector contains exactly the points equally distant from B and C.
Any intersection satisfies both conditions, though the construction may give zero, one, or two points.

solutions.question: There is an apple tree at a distance of 90 metres from banana tree in the garden of Sara’s house. Sara wants to plant a mango tree M which is 64 metres from apple tree and between 54 and 82 metres from the banana tree. Using a scale of 1cm to represent 10m, Find the points where the mango tree should be planted.
steps: Using the given scale, represent 90 m by 9 cm. Draw AB = 9 cm, where A is the apple tree and B is the banana tree.
Represent 64 m by 6.4 cm. With A as centre and radius 6.4 cm, draw a circle.
Represent 54 m by 5.4 cm. With B as centre and radius 5.4 cm, draw a circle.
Represent 82 m by 8.2 cm. With B as centre and radius 8.2 cm, draw a circle.
Mark the portions of the circle centred at A that lie outside the 5.4 cm circle and inside the 8.2 cm circle centred at B.
solutions.answer: The mango tree may be planted at any point on the parts of the circle centred at A with radius 6.4 cm that are between 5.4 cm and 8.2 cm from B.
solutions.figure: The possible planting positions lie on the parts of the circle centred at A with radius 6.4 cm that are between the circles centred at the banana tree with radii 5.4 cm and 8.2 cm. The intersections of these circles mark the ends of the allowed arcs.
why: The scale converts the tree separation into a drawing length and labels each tree’s location.
The circle gives every point 64 m from the apple tree.
The circle marks the minimum allowed distance from the banana tree.
The larger circle marks the maximum allowed distance from the banana tree.
The qualifying arcs satisfy both banana-distance limits while remaining 64 m from the apple tree.

modules.title: Unit 11 review

bookReference.text: Your textbook, Unit 11, review exercise, pages 213–214; Review Exercise 11

readingTasks: Revise Unit 11 and attempt Review Exercise 11 (pages 213–214).

examTips: Review questions may ask you to choose a locus from a condition, state a triangle property, or construct a triangle and its locus.
In construction questions, show the construction lines clearly and label the given lengths, angles, vertices, and locus.
Marks are commonly earned for the correctly constructed base, accurate angles or lengths, the correct third vertex, and the correctly drawn locus.
For a region question, show the boundary and make clear which side or interior region satisfies the condition.

hints: Draw AB = 5.3 cm first.
Draw the 30° ray at A and the 120° ray at B on the same side of AB; their meeting point is C. Then construct the perpendicular bisector of AB.
yourTurn.question:
Construct a triangle ABC with mA̅B̅ = 5.3 cm, m∠A = 30° and m∠B = 120°.
Draw the locus of all points which are equidistant from A and B.
solution: At A, construct a ray making an angle of 30° with AB.
At B, construct a ray making an angle of 120° with BA on the same side of AB.
Label the intersection of the rays C and join AC and BC.
With A and B as centres and equal radii greater than half of AB, draw arcs above and below AB.
Join the two arc-intersection points; this line is the perpendicular bisector of AB and is the required locus.
yourTurn.answer: Triangle ABC is constructed with AB = 5.3 cm, ∠A = 30° and ∠B = 120°. Its required locus is the perpendicular bisector of AB.

steps.why: The 8 cm side is a convenient base, and the 6 cm side can be erected perpendicular to it.
A right angle between the 8 cm and 6 cm sides makes the triangle right angled.
steps.text: At B, construct a perpendicular to AB.

steps.why: This fixes the second leg at the required length.
steps.text: On the perpendicular, mark C so that BC = 6 cm.

steps.why: Joining the remaining endpoints completes the triangle; its hypotenuse is 10 cm.
steps.text: Join A to C; AC = 10 cm.

example.question: Construct a right angled triangle with measures of sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm.
example.answer: A right angled triangle ABC is constructed with AB = 8 cm, BC = 6 cm, ∠B = 90° and AC = 10 cm.

explain.title: Triangle construction condition
explain.body: A triangle can be constructed only when the sum of any two side lengths is greater than the third side. An equilateral triangle has all sides equal and all angles 60°; it is also isosceles.

explain.title: Triangle facts and special segments
explain.body: The angles of a triangle add to 180°. A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. The three internal angle bisectors meet at one point.

explain.title: Locus from a fixed point or line
explain.body: Points at a fixed distance from one point lie on a circle centred at that point. Points at a fixed distance from a straight line lie on parallel lines, one on each side.

explain.title: Locus from equal distances
explain.body: Points equidistant from two fixed points lie on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them. Points equidistant from two intersecting lines lie on their angle bisectors.

explain.title: Showing a required region
explain.body: Convert real distances using the given scale before drawing. For example, 32 m at 1 cm to 10 m is 3.2 cm. For a region, identify its boundary first, then shade or mark the side that meets the words such as inside, less than, or farther than.

mistakes: Using a side-sum equal to the third side; it must be strictly greater.
Drawing an angle at the wrong endpoint or measuring it from the wrong arm.
Confusing the perpendicular bisector of a segment with an angle bisector.
Forgetting that a fixed-distance locus from a point is a circle centred at that point.
Using the scale backwards or shading the wrong side of a locus boundary.

recap.question: What is the locus of points equidistant from E and F?
What is the locus of points 5 cm from a fixed point A?
recap.answer: A circle centred at A with radius 5 cm

solutions.question: Construct a right angled triangle with measures of sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm.
steps: Draw a line segment AB = 8 cm.
At A, construct a perpendicular to AB.
With centre A and radius 6 cm, draw an arc cutting the perpendicular at C.
The triangle ABC is the required right-angled triangle; its sides are AB = 8 cm, AC = 6 cm and BC = 10 cm.
solutions.answer: The required right-angled triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm.
solutions.figure: A right-angled triangle with perpendicular sides 8 cm and 6 cm, and hypotenuse 10 cm.
why: The 8 cm side provides a base for constructing the triangle.
A perpendicular creates the right angle required for a 6-8-10 triangle.
The arc marks a point 6 cm from A on the perpendicular.
The joining side has length 10 cm by the Pythagorean theorem.
The side lengths verify the construction, since 6² + 8² = 10².

solutions.question: Construct a triangle ABC with mA̅B̅ = 5.3 cm, m∠A = 30° and m∠B = 120°. Draw the locus of all points which are equidistant from A and B.
steps: At A, construct a ray making an angle of 30° with AB.
At B, construct a ray making an angle of 120° with BA, on the same side of AB as the ray at A.
Mark the intersection of the two rays as C.
Join AC and BC to complete triangle ABC.
With centres A and B and the same radius greater than half of AB, draw arcs above and below AB to intersect at P and Q.
PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB and is the required locus.
solutions.answer: Triangle ABC is constructed, and its required locus is the perpendicular bisector of AB.
solutions.figure: Triangle ABC with AB = 5.3 cm, ∠A = 30° and ∠B = 120°. The perpendicular bisector of AB is also drawn as the locus equidistant from A and B.
why: The given length establishes the base of the triangle.
This ray fixes the direction of side AC.
The second ray fixes side BC and forms the specified angle with BA.
The rays’ intersection determines the third vertex.
Joining the sides completes the required triangle.
Equal-radius arcs locate points equally distant from A and B.
The line through the arc intersections is their perpendicular bisector.
Every point on this line is equidistant from A and B, so it is the required locus.

solutions.question: Construct a triangle with mD̅E̅ = 7.3 cm, m∠D = 42° and mE̅F̅ = 5.4 cm.
steps: At D, construct a ray making an angle of 42° with DE.
With centre E and radius 5.4 cm, draw an arc cutting the ray at F.
solutions.answer: Triangle DEF is constructed with DE = 7.3 cm, ∠D = 42° and EF = 5.4 cm.
solutions.figure: Triangle DEF with DE = 7.3 cm, ∠D = 42° and EF = 5.4 cm. The arc from E may meet the angle ray at two points; either intersection gives a valid construction.
why: The given side length provides the triangle’s base.
The ray fixes the direction of the side starting at D.
The arc marks a point 5.4 cm from E on the ray.
Joining the points forms the remaining side.
The constructed sides and angle match the required measurements.

solutions.question: Construct a triangle XYZ with mY̅X̅ = 8 cm, mY̅Z̅ = 7 cm and mX̅Z̅ = 6.5 cm. Draw the locus of all points which are equidistant from X̅Y̅ and X̅Z̅.
steps: With centre X and radius 6.5 cm, draw an arc; with centre Y and radius 7 cm, draw an arc intersecting it at Z.
Join XZ and YZ to construct △XYZ.
With centre X, draw an arc cutting XY and XZ; from those two cut points draw equal-radius arcs meeting inside ∠YXZ, then join their intersection to X to draw the internal angle bisector.
Through X, construct a line perpendicular to the internal angle bisector; this is the external angle bisector.
The internal and external angle bisectors give the locus of points equidistant from XY and XZ.
solutions.answer: The locus is the pair of angle bisectors of ∠YXZ: its internal and external angle bisectors.
solutions.figure: Triangle XYZ with XY = 8 cm, YZ = 7 cm and XZ = 6.5 cm. The internal bisector of ∠YXZ is drawn as the locus equidistant from XY and XZ.
accept: The locus is the pair of angle bisectors of ∠YXZ: its internal and external angle bisectors.

solutions.question: Construct a triangle FGH such that mF̅G̅ = mG̅H̅ = 6.4 cm, m∠G = 122°.
steps: At G, construct an angle of 122° and draw its two rays.
With centre G and radius 6.4 cm, mark F on one ray and H on the other ray.
Join F to H to complete triangle FGH.
solutions.answer: Triangle FGH is constructed with FG = GH = 6.4 cm and ∠FGH = 122°.
solutions.figure: Isosceles triangle FGH with FG = GH = 6.4 cm and ∠FGH = 122°.
why: The given angle fixes the direction of both equal sides.
A radius of 6.4 cm sets both required side lengths from G.
The final side closes the triangle.

solutions.question: Construct a triangle FGH such that mF̅G̅ = mG̅H̅ = 6.4 cm, m∠G = 122°. Draw the locus of all points which are: (a) equidistant from F and G,
steps: At G, construct an angle of 122° and draw its two rays.
With centre G and radius 6.4 cm, mark F on one ray and H on the other ray.
Join F to H to complete triangle FGH.
With centres F and G and the same radius greater than half of FG, draw arcs on both sides of FG to intersect at P and Q.
PQ is the perpendicular bisector of FG and is the required locus.
solutions.answer: Triangle FGH is constructed, and the perpendicular bisector of FG is the required locus.
solutions.figure: Isosceles triangle FGH with FG = GH = 6.4 cm and ∠FGH = 122°. The perpendicular bisector of FG is drawn as the locus equidistant from F and G.
why: The given angle fixes the directions of the two equal sides.
The compass radius sets both side lengths to 6.4 cm.
Joining the remaining vertices completes the triangle.
Equal-radius arcs from F and G locate points equally distant from F and G.
The line through the two arc intersections is perpendicular to FG.
Every point on a perpendicular bisector is equally distant from the segment’s endpoints.

solutions.question: Construct a triangle FGH such that mF̅G̅ = mG̅H̅ = 6.4 cm, m∠G = 122°. Draw the locus of all points which are: (b) equidistant from F̅G̅ and G̅H̅.
steps: At G, construct an angle of 122° with GF as one arm.
On the other arm, mark H so that GH = 6.4 cm; join F to H to construct △FGH.
With centre G, draw an arc cutting GF and GH; from those two cut points draw equal-radius arcs meeting inside ∠FGH, then join their intersection to G to draw the internal angle bisector.
Through G, construct a line perpendicular to the internal angle bisector; this is the external angle bisector.
The internal and external angle bisectors give the locus of points equidistant from FG and GH.
solutions.answer: The locus is the pair of angle bisectors of ∠FGH: its internal and external angle bisectors.
solutions.figure: Isosceles triangle FGH with FG = GH = 6.4 cm and ∠FGH = 122°. The internal bisector of ∠FGH is drawn as the locus equidistant from FG and GH.
accept: The locus is the pair of angle bisectors of ∠FGH: its internal and external angle bisectors.

solutions.question: Construct a triangle FGH such that mF̅G̅ = mG̅H̅ = 6.4 cm, m∠G = 122°. Draw the locus of all points which are: (c) Mark the point where the two loci intersect.
steps: At G, construct an angle of 122° and draw its two rays.
With centre G and radius 6.4 cm, mark F on one ray and H on the other ray.
Join F to H to complete triangle FGH.
With centres F and G and the same radius greater than half of FG, draw arcs on both sides of FG to intersect at A and B.
Draw the straight line AB to construct the perpendicular bisector of FG.
With centre G and a convenient radius, draw an arc cutting GF and GH at C and D.
With centres C and D and equal radii, draw arcs intersecting at E inside ∠FGH.
Draw the internal bisector GE of ∠FGH.
Mark the intersection of AB and GE as P.
solutions.answer: P, the intersection of the perpendicular bisector of FG and the internal bisector of ∠FGH, is the required point.
solutions.figure: Triangle FGH with the perpendicular bisector of FG and the internal bisector of ∠FGH drawn. Their intersection is marked P.
why: The given angle fixes the directions of the two equal sides.
The compass radius sets both side lengths to 6.4 cm.
Joining F and H completes the triangle.
Equal-radius arcs from F and G locate points equally distant from the endpoints.
The line through the arc intersections constructs the perpendicular bisector.
The arc marks equal distances from the two arms of the angle.
Intersecting equal-radius arcs create a point equidistant from C and D.
The line from the vertex through the arc intersection bisects the angle.
The crossing point satisfies both locus conditions.

solutions.question: Two houses Q and R are 73 metres apart. Using a scale of 1 cm to represent 10 m, construct the locus of a point P which moves such that it is: (i) at a distance of 32 metres from Q
steps: Draw QR = 7.3 cm to represent the 73 m distance between the houses.
Using Q as centre and a radius of 3.2 cm (representing 32 m), draw a circle.
Every point on this circle is 32 m from Q, so the circle is the required locus.
solutions.answer: The locus is a circle centred at Q with radius 3.2 cm.
solutions.figure: A circle with centre Q and radius 3.2 cm, drawn around Q. This is the locus of P.
why: The scale converts the real separation into a drawing length: 73 ÷ 10 = 7.3 cm.
The scale converts 32 m into 3.2 cm, and a circle marks all points that distance from Q.
A circle’s points are all the same radius from its centre, matching the condition.

solutions.question: Two houses Q and R are 73 metres apart. Using a scale of 1 cm to represent 10 m, construct the locus of a point P which moves such that it is: (ii) at a distance of 48 metres from the line joining Q and R.
steps: Draw QR = 7.3 cm to represent the 73 m distance between the houses.
At Q and R, construct perpendiculars to QR.
On the perpendiculars, mark points 4.8 cm from QR on the same side of QR, and join these points to draw a line parallel to QR.
Repeat on the other side of QR, marking points 4.8 cm from QR and joining them to draw the second parallel line.
Extend both parallel lines as required. Each is 4.8 cm from QR, so together they form the required locus.
solutions.answer: The locus is the pair of lines parallel to QR and 4.8 cm from QR, one on each side.
solutions.figure: Two lines parallel to QR, each 4.8 cm from QR, one on either side. These lines form the locus of P.
why: The scale converts the real separation into its drawing length.
Perpendiculars provide directions measured at right angles to QR.
The scale converts 48 m to 4.8 cm, and parallel lines keep that distance from QR.
The opposite-side line includes points equally far from QR on the other side.
Both lines contain exactly the points 4.8 cm from QR.

solutions.question: The field is in the form of a rectangle ABCD with mA̅B̅ = 70m and mB̅C̅ = 60 m. Construct the rectangle ABCD using a scale of 1cm to represent 10 m. Show the region inside the field which is less than 30 m from C and farther than 25 m from A̅B̅.
steps: Draw AB = 7 cm to represent 70 m.
At B, construct a perpendicular to AB and mark BC = 6 cm to represent 60 m.
Through C, draw a line parallel to AB; through A, draw a line parallel to BC. Let these lines meet at D to complete rectangle ABCD.
At a distance of 2.5 cm from AB, draw a line parallel to AB inside the rectangle; this represents the line 25 m from AB.
With C as centre and radius 3 cm, draw the arc inside the rectangle; this represents points 30 m from C.
The points inside the rectangle and less than 3 cm from C lie inside this quarter-circle. They are all more than 2.5 cm from AB, since the nearest point of the quarter-circle to AB is 3 cm from AB.
Shade the region inside the quarter-circle and within the rectangle to show the required region.
solutions.answer: The required region is the part of the rectangle inside the quarter-circle centred at C with radius 3 cm.
solutions.figure: Rectangle ABCD measuring 7 cm by 6 cm. Inside it, the required region is the part of the quarter-circle centred at C with radius 3 cm; shade the region inside the arc. Also show the line parallel to AB and 2.5 cm from AB. The shaded region lies farther than 2.5 cm from AB.
why: The scale converts 70 m into 7 cm on the drawing.
A rectangle has right angles, and the scale converts 60 m into 6 cm.
Parallel opposite sides complete a rectangle with the required dimensions.
The scale converts 25 m into 2.5 cm, marking the boundary of the distance condition.
The scale converts 30 m into 3 cm, marking points exactly 30 m from C.
The required points must be inside the 30 m boundary and beyond the 25 m boundary.
Shading highlights the points satisfying both distance conditions inside the field.

definitions.text: Scalene triangle: All sides are of different length.
Isosceles triangles: Two sides are of equal length.
Equilateral triangle: All sides of equal length.
Acute angled triangle: All angles are of measure less than 90⁰.
Obtuse angled triangle: One angle is of measure greater than 90⁰.
Right angled triangle: One angle is of measure equal to 90⁰.
A triangle is a closed figure having three sides and three angles.
The sum of the measure of any two sides of a triangle is always greater than the measure of the third side.
The Ambiguous Case (SSA) occurs when we are given two sides and the angle opposite one of these is less than 90°.

A perpendicular bisector is a line that intersects a line segment at right angle and dividing it into two equal parts. In other words, it intersects the line segment at its midpoint and forms right angles (90°) with it.
A median of a triangle is a line segment that joins a vertex to the midpoint of the side that is opposite to that vertex.

A point of concurrency is the single point where three or more lines, rays or line segments intersect or meet in a geometric figure. This concept is commonly used in triangles, where several important types of points of concurrency exist.
The point of concurrency of perpendicular bisector of the sides of a triangle is called circumcentre.
The point of concurrency of the medians of a triangle is called centroid of the triangle.
An angle bisector of a triangle is a line or ray that divides an angle into two equal parts, creating two smaller angles that are congruent (each having half the measure of the original angle).
The point of concurrency of the angle bisectors of a triangle is called incentre of the triangle.

Altitude is a ray drawn perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side of the triangle. There are three altitudes of the triangle which meet at a single point i.e. the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent.

A locus (plural loci) is a set of points that follow a given rule. In geometry, loci are often used to define the positions of points relative to one another or to other geometric figures. Some common types of loci along with detailed explanations will be discussed.
Equidistant: Let A be a fixed point and B be a set of points. If A is at equal distance from all points of B, then A is said to be equidistant from B.
The locus of a point whose distance is constant from a fixed point is called a circle.

The locus of a point whose distance from a fixed line is constant are parallel lines, ℓ and m e. g. the locus of a point P whose distance is 2.5 cm from a fixed line AB are parallel lines at a distance of 2.5 cm from AB.
The locus of a point whose distance from two fixed points is constant is called a perpendicular bisector.
The locus of a point whose distance is constant from two intersecting lines is called an angle bisector.
If two or more loci intersect at a point P, then P satisfies all given conditions of the loci.

explain.title: Ungrouped and grouped data
explain.body: Data which is not arranged in any systematic order (groups or classes) is called ungrouped data. When the same data is arranged into groups or classes, it is called grouped data.

explain.title: Frequency distribution
explain.body: A distribution or table that represents classes or groups along with their respective class frequencies is called frequency distribution. The frequency tells how many data values fall in each class.

explain.title: Making class intervals
explain.body: First find the range by subtracting the smallest value from the greatest value. Divide the range by the desired number of classes to find the class size, then form the class limits and count the data with tally marks.

explain.title: Unequal class widths
explain.body: When the class widths are unequal, adjust each rectangle height by dividing its class frequency by its class width. These proportional heights are also called adjusted frequencies.

explain.title: Midpoints and frequency polygons
explain.body: A frequency polygon is a line graph of a frequency distribution in which frequencies are plotted against their midpoints. Midpoint is the average value of the lower and upper class limits.

mistakes: Using the range formula in the wrong order: subtract the smallest value from the greatest value.
Starting the class intervals at a value other than the smallest data value when following the textbook method.
Counting a value twice or missing it while making tally marks.
Using the original frequencies as histogram heights when class widths are unequal; divide each frequency by its class width.
Using class limits instead of midpoints for the horizontal values of a frequency polygon.
Forgetting to label axes, state a scale, or join the polygon points with straight lines.

explain.title: What is central tendency?
explain.body: The measure that gives the centre of the data is called measure of central tendency. Therefore, measure of central tendency is used to find out the middle or central value of a data set. It gives one representative value for a whole set of data.

explain.title: Arithmetic mean
explain.body: It is defined as a value of variable which is obtained by dividing the sum of all the values (observations) by their number of observations. For ungrouped data, use x̄ = Σx/n. For grouped data, use x̄ = Σfx/Σf, where x is the midpoint of each class.

explain.title: Median
explain.body: Median is the middle most value in an arranged (ascending or descending order) data set. Median is the value which divides the data into two equal parts i.e., 50% data is before the median and 50% data after it. For grouped data, find cumulative frequencies, locate the n/2-th item and use Median = ℓ + (h/f)(n/2 − c).

explain.title: Mode and weighted mean
explain.body: In a data the values (observation) which appears or occurs most often is called mode of the data. It is the most common value. When observations have different weights, use weighted mean: x̄w = ΣWX/ΣW.

mistakes: Finding a median without arranging ungrouped observations first.
For an even number of values, choosing one middle value instead of averaging the two middle values.
Using class limits instead of class midpoints when finding a grouped arithmetic mean.
For a grouped median, using the wrong cumulative frequency: c is the cumulative frequency before the median class.
For grouped mode, mixing up f1 (the preceding frequency) and f2 (the following frequency).
For weighted mean, dividing by the number of values instead of by the sum of the weights.
Leaving out units or rounding before completing the calculation.

explain.title: Frequency and frequency distributions
explain.body: Frequency is the number of times a value occurs. A frequency distribution organises data into values or classes and records their frequencies.

explain.title: Histograms and frequency polygons
explain.body: A histogram displays frequencies with adjoining rectangles. To make a frequency polygon, plot frequencies at class midpoints and join the points; it can also be drawn on a histogram.

explain.title: Class boundaries and midpoints
explain.body: For integer class limits, class boundaries make neighbouring intervals join. The midpoint, or class mark, is the average of the two class limits.

explain.title: Mean and weighted mean
explain.body: The mean is the sum of observations divided by their number. For a frequency distribution, use Σfx ÷ Σf; for weighted data, the weights determine how much each value contributes.

explain.title: Median, mode and range
explain.body: Arrange data to find the median: choose the middle value, or average the two middle values. The mode occurs most often. The range is the greatest value minus the smallest value.

definitions.text: Information handling is the process of collecting, organizing, summarizing, analyzing and interpreting numerical data.
So, the collection of meaningful information in the form of facts and numerical figures is known as data.

It can take only some specific values. whole numbers are used to write discrete data. e.g., number of books sold by a shopkeeper, number of patients visited a hospital in a week etc. This data is only obtained by counting.

It can take every possible value in a given interval. Decimal numbers are used to write continuous data. The data is only obtained by measuring e.g., the mass of students in class i.e., 28.5 kg, 26.5 kg, 27.5 kg etc.
Data which is not arranged in any systematic order (groups or classes) is called ungrouped data.
If we arrange the above given data in groups or classes, then it is called grouped data.
Range is the difference between the greatest value and the smallest value i.e., Range = Xₘₐₓ − Xₘᵢₙ
The number of times a value occurs in a data is called the frequency of that value. It is denoted by “f”.

This is a graph of adjacent rectangles constructed on xy plane. A histogram is similar to bar graph but it is constructed for a frequency distribution. In a histogram, the values of the data (classes) are represented along the horizontal axis and the frequencies are shown by bars perpendicular to the horizontal axis. Bars of equal width are used to represent individual classes of frequency table.

A frequency polygon is a closed geometrical figure used to display a frequency distribution graphically. A line graph of a frequency distribution is known as frequency polygon in which frequencies are plotted against their midpoints.
Midpoint is the average value of the lower and upper class limits. Midpoint is also known as class mark.
The measure that gives the centre of the data is called measure of central tendency. Therefore, measure of central tendency is used to find out the middle or central value of a data set.
It is defined as a value of variable which is obtained by dividing the sum of all the values (observations) by their number of observations.

Median is the middle most value in an arranged (ascending or descending order) data set. Median is the value which divides the data into two equal parts i.e., 50% data is before the median and 50% data after it. Median is denoted by X̃.
In a data the values (observation) which appears or occurs most often is called mode of the data. It is the most common value. Mode is denoted by X̂.

Arithmetic Mean is used when all the observations are given equal importance / weight but there are certain situations in which the different observations get different weights. In this situation, weighted mean denoted by X̄_w is preferred.

fullMarks: For a frequency table, show the range and class-size calculation first; then make clear columns for class limits, tally marks, frequency and class boundaries when required.
For a histogram, label both axes, mark class boundaries on the horizontal axis, use a stated scale and draw adjoining rectangles. For unequal class widths, calculate and use adjusted frequencies.
For a frequency polygon, show the midpoint calculation, plot each midpoint against its frequency, join the points with straight lines and extend both ends to the x-axis.
For a grouped mean, include columns for midpoint x and fx (or deviation D and fD); show Σf and Σfx (or ΣfD) before substituting into the formula.
For an ungrouped median, arrange all values in ascending or descending order and state the observation position before giving the answer. For even n, average the two middle observations.
For a grouped median, show the cumulative-frequency column, identify the median class and state ℓ, h, f, n and c before substitution.
For a grouped mode, identify the modal class and clearly state ℓ, h, fₘ, f₁ and f₂. Finish with a sentence giving the answer and its units when the data has units.

Finding the median before arranging raw data, or choosing the wrong middle position. Arrange the values first and then use the odd- or even-number formula.
Using the wrong cumulative frequency in the grouped-median formula. Use c as the cumulative frequency before the median class, not the cumulative frequency of that class.
Mixing up the modal-class frequency and its neighbouring frequencies. Use fₘ for the modal class, f₁ for the class before it and f₂ for the class after it.

shortTheory.question: Define frequency distribution.
shortTheory.answer: A distribution or table that represents classes or groups along with their respective class frequencies is called frequency distribution. In other words, the various items of data are classified into certain groups or classes and the number of items lying in each group or class is put against that group or class. The data organised and summarized in this way is known as frequency distribution.

shortTheory.question: Define median.

shortTheory.question: Define mode.

explain.title: Probability
explain.body: “Probability is the chance of occurrence of a particular event.” It is calculated using P(A) = n(A)/n(S), where n(A) is the number of favourable outcomes and n(S) is the total number of possible outcomes.

explain.title: Experiment, outcomes, and sample space
explain.body: “The process which generates results e.g., tossing a coin, rolling a dice, etc. is called an experiment.” “The results of an experiment are called outcomes.” “The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment is called sample space.” The textbook denotes the sample space by S.

explain.title: Favourable outcome and event

explain.title: Probability limits and event types
explain.body: The range of probability is 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1. A certain event has probability 1, and an impossible event has probability 0. Likely and unlikely describe events with greater or lesser chances of occurring.

explain.title: The complement
explain.body: The probability of not getting head while tossing a coin is known as the complement of that event. More generally, the complement of event A is the event that A does not occur.

explain.title: The complement formula
explain.body: The complement of an event “A” is calculated by the given formula: P(A') = 1 − P(A). Subtract the probability of the event from 1.

explain.title: Event and complement add to 1
explain.body: The sum of the probability of an event “A” and the probability of an event not occurring “A” is always “1”. P(A) + P(A′) = 1.

solutions.question: Taabish tossed a fair coin and rolled a fair dice once. Find the probability of the following events: not tail on coin and the number 5 on dice.
steps: A coin and a die have 2 × 6 = 12 equally likely outcomes.

The supplied answer 11/12 interprets the event as the complement of getting (T, 5).
All outcomes except (T, 5) are favourable under this interpretation, so P = 11/12.

solutions.question: Taabish tossed a fair coin and rolled a fair dice once. Find the probability of the following events: not head on coin and the number 5 and 2 on dice.
steps: A coin and a die have 2 × 6 = 12 equally likely outcomes.

The supplied answer 5/6 interprets the event as the complement of getting head with either 5 or 2.
The two excluded outcomes are (H, 5) and (H, 2), leaving 12 − 2 = 10 favourable outcomes.

accept: 5/6 (the supplied book answer, under the complement interpretation; if “not head” means tail, the probability is 1/6).

solutions.question: A card is selected at random from a well shuffled pack of 52 plying cards. What will be the probability of selecting: neither a queen nor a jack.
steps: Number of queens = 4 and number of jacks = 4.

explain.title: Probability of an event

explain.title: Events that are not wanted
explain.body: For an event described with “not”, count outcomes outside the event. For example, the cards that are neither jacks nor kings are the other 44 cards in a 52-card pack, so the probability is 44/52 = 11/13.

explain.title: Relative frequency
explain.body: Relative frequency compares the observed frequency of an event with the total number of trials. Divide each frequency by the total frequency; the relative frequencies for all categories together add to 1.

explain.title: Expected frequency

definitions.text: Hence, Probability is the chance of occurrence of a particular event.
The process which generates results e.g., tossing a coin, rolling a dice, etc. is called an experiment.
The results of an experiment are called outcomes e.g., the possible outcomes of tossing a coin are head or tail, the possible outcomes of rolling a dice are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

An outcome which represents how many times we expect the things to be happened e.g., while tossing a coin, there is 1 favourable outcome of getting head or tail. While rolling a dice, there are 3 favourable outcomes of getting multiples of 2 i.e. {2, 4, 6}

The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment is called sample space. It is denoted by ‘S’ e.g., while tossing a coin, the sample space will be S = {H, T}. While rolling a dice, the sample space will be S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
Each element of the sample space is called sample point.
The set of results of an experiment is called an event e.g., while rolling a dice getting even number is an event i.e., A = {2, 4, 6}; n(A) = 3.
An event which is sure to occur. The probability of sure event is 1.
An event cannot occur in any trial. The probability of this event is 0.
An event which will probably occur. It has greater chance to occur.
An event which will not probably occur. It has less chance to occur.
The events which have equal chance of occurrence. The probability of these events is 0.5.
The probability of not getting head while tossing a coin is known as the complement of that event.
Relative frequency tells us how often a specific event occurs relative to the total number of frequency event or trials.
Expected frequency is a measure that estimate how often an event should be occurred depended on probability.

For a pair of dice, treat the results as ordered pairs and use 36 total outcomes; do not count (2, 5) and (5, 2) as the same outcome.

mistakes: Using only the different labels in a word instead of counting repeated letters. Fix: count every letter position in the word for the total and favourable outcomes.
Treating two-dice results as unordered pairs. Fix: keep the dice order fixed; for example, (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different outcomes.
Forgetting that “at least” includes the stated number. Fix: list all values equal to or greater than the number given.
Finding the probability of an event but not its complement when the question asks “not.” Fix: calculate 1 − P(A) and state the requested probability.
Using the frequency of one category as the total when calculating relative frequency. Fix: add all frequencies first to get N = Σf.
Reporting a percentage as a relative frequency without converting it to a decimal or fraction. Fix: give frequency ÷ total as a fraction or decimal, and label a percentage clearly if requested.
Multiplying the probability by the event count instead of the number of trials for expected frequency. Fix: use expected frequency = N × P(A), where N is the total number of trials.

notes.title: Recognising Rational and Irrational Numbers
notes.answer: A real number is either rational or irrational.
notes.explanation: Real numbers include both rational and irrational numbers. A rational number can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. An irrational number cannot be written as a quotient of integers. Terminating and recurring decimals are rational; non-terminating, non-recurring decimals are irrational.
notes.simple: A decimal that ends or repeats is rational. A decimal that goes on forever without repeating is irrational.
examples: 0.25 is a terminating decimal, so it is rational.
0.333... is recurring, so it is rational.
steps: If it does not end, check whether its digits repeat.
A terminating or recurring decimal is rational.
A non-terminating, non-recurring decimal is irrational.
notes.checkQuestion: Is 0.272727... rational or irrational?
notes.checkAnswer: Irrational: it is non-terminating and non-recurring.

notes.title: Radicals, surds, and rationalizing denominators
notes.answer: For 3/(√5 + √2), multiply the numerator and denominator by √5 − √2.
notes.explanation: A radical is another way to write a root. To simplify radicals, use the laws of radicals and indices. To rationalize a denominator with two terms, multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate.
notes.simple: A surd is an irrational root of a rational number. If a denominator has a sum or difference of two terms, use its conjugate to remove the radical from the denominator.
examples: √5 is a surd; √9 is not a surd because it simplifies to 3.
The conjugate of √5 + √2 is √5 − √2.
steps: Identify the radical and its index.
Use the laws of radicals and indices to simplify roots and powers.
For a two-term radical denominator, multiply top and bottom by its conjugate.
notes.checkQuestion: What should you multiply by to rationalize 3/(√5 + √2)?
notes.checkAnswer: Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.

notes.answer: Real numbers can be used to solve everyday problems such as temperature conversion, profit and loss, tax, and sharing profit in a given ratio.

notes.answer: Real numbers include rational and irrational numbers, and their properties help us simplify expressions and solve problems.
