rubric.why: Identifies the purpose of scientific notation.
rubric.description: A method for expressing very large or very small numbers.
rubric.how: Award for identifying that it is a method used to express large or small numbers; either size qualifies if paired with expressing numbers as a method. The statement need not use the exact textbook wording yet. The second point covers expressing them in a manageable form and naming the method scientific notation. Do not award this point for merely saying it is used in science or mathematics; that is an application, not the definition’s key purpose.

rubric.why: Completes the definition by stating the form’s purpose and name.
rubric.description: It expresses numbers in a more manageable form and is known as scientific notation.
rubric.how: Award when the answer identifies a manageable form and names scientific notation. Accept equivalent wording such as easier-to-handle form. The first point covers the method and the very large or very small numbers it expresses; this point completes the definition.

written.text: What is a common logarithm?
modelAnswer: The common logarithm is the logarithm with a base of 10. It is written as log_10 or simply as log (when no base is mentioned, it is usually assumed to be base 10).

rubric.why: Identifies the defining base of a common logarithm.

rubric.description: It is written log₁₀ or log; an unmarked log is usually understood to have base 10.
rubric.how: Award for either log₁₀ notation or stating that log without a base is assumed to mean base 10. The first point covers the defining base itself.

written.text: Define the characteristic of a logarithm.
modelAnswer: The characteristic is the integral part of the logarithm. It tells us how big or small the number is.

rubric.how: Award when the answer says the characteristic indicates the number’s size, such as how big or small it is. The first point covers its definition as the integral part.

written.text: Define the mantissa of a logarithm.
modelAnswer: The mantissa is the decimal part of the logarithm. It represents the "fractional" component and is always positive.

written.text: What is an antilogarithm?

written.text: Prove that (1 + sin θ)/(1 − sin θ) − (1 − sin θ)/(1 + sin θ) = 2 Cosec θ.

A proof is a logical argument that establishes the truth of a mathematical statement.
Example 1: “2 + 3 = 5” is a statement; arithmetic showing that 2 + 3 = 5 is its proof.
Example 2: “The sum of the interior angles of a triangle is 180°” is a statement; a valid geometric argument establishing it is its proof.

written.text: Prove that the bisectors of the angles of a triangle are concurrent.

Hence I lies on the bisector of ∠C.
Thus the three angle bisectors of △ABC pass through the same point I and are concurrent.

written.text: Prove that the bisectors of the angles of a triangle are concurrent. OR Prove that triangles on equal bases and of equal altitudes are equal in area.
modelAnswer: To prove that the bisectors of the angles of a triangle are concurrent:
Let the bisectors of ∠A and ∠B intersect at I.
Since I lies on the bisector of ∠A, d(I,AB)=d(I,AC).
Since I lies on the bisector of ∠B, d(I,AB)=d(I,BC).
Therefore, d(I,AC)=d(I,BC), so I lies on bisector ∠C.
Hence all three angle bisectors are concurrent.
To prove that triangles on equal bases and of equal altitudes are equal in area:
Let b1 and b2 be the base lengths, and h1 and h2 the corresponding altitudes.
Area of the first triangle, A1=1/2 b1h1.
Area of the second triangle, A2=1/2 b2h2.
Therefore, A1=A2, so the triangles are equal in area.

written.text: Prove that the right bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent. OR Prove that triangles on equal bases and of equal altitudes are equal in area.
modelAnswer: Let the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC meet at O.
Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, OA = OB.
Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC, OA = OC.
Therefore, OB = OC, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC.
Hence the perpendicular bisectors of the three sides are concurrent at O.
Let the equal bases of the two triangles be b1 and b2, and their equal altitudes be h1 and h2.
Thus b1 = b2 and h1 = h2.
Area of the first triangle, A1 = 1/2 × b1 × h1.
Area of the second triangle, A2 = 1/2 × b2 × h2.
Since b1 = b2 and h1 = h2, A1 = A2.
Hence the triangles are equal in area.

written.text: Prove that the right bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent. OR Prove that triangles on the same base and of the same (i.e. equal) altitudes are equal in area.
modelAnswer: Proof 1: Right bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent.
Let the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC meet at O.
Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, OA = OB.
Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC, OB = OC.
Hence, O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC.
Thus, the perpendicular bisectors of all three sides pass through O and are concurrent.
Proof 2: Triangles on the same base and with equal altitudes have equal areas.
Let the two triangles have the same base b and equal altitudes h.
Area of the first triangle = 1/2 bh.
Area of the second triangle = 1/2 bh.
Therefore, the areas of the two triangles are equal.

modelAnswer: Option 1: Let the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC meet at O.
Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, OA = OB.

written.text: Prove that “The right bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent.” OR Prove that “triangles on the same base and of same (i.e. equal) altitudes are equal in area.”
modelAnswer: Option 1: Let the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC meet at O.
Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, OA = OB.
Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC, OA = OC.
Therefore OB = OC, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC.
Hence the right bisectors of the three sides are concurrent.
Option 2: Let the triangles have common base b and equal altitudes h.
Area of the first triangle = 1/2 bh.
Area of the second triangle = 1/2 bh.
Therefore, the two triangles are equal in area.

written.text: Prove that the right bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent. OR Prove that parallelograms on equal bases and having the same (or equal) altitudes are equal in area.
modelAnswer: Option 1: Concurrency of the perpendicular bisectors
Let the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC meet at O.
Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, OA = OB.
Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC, OB = OC.
Therefore OA = OC, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC.
Hence the three perpendicular bisectors pass through O and are concurrent.
Area of a parallelogram = base × altitude.
Let the equal bases of the two parallelograms be b and their equal altitudes be h.
Their areas are b × h and b × h.
Therefore, the parallelograms are equal in area.

written.text: Construct a right angled isosceles triangle whose hypotenuse is 5.2 cm long.
modelAnswer: Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB, meeting AB at its midpoint M; hence AM = MB = 2.6 cm.

Join AC and BC. Since CM ⟂ AB and M is the midpoint of AB, AC = BC and ∠ACB = 90°.

written.text: Construct the triangle ABC. Draw the bisectors of its angles and verify their concurrency: mAB = 4.2 cm, mBC = 6 cm, mCA = 5.2 cm.
modelAnswer: With centre A and radius 5.2 cm, draw an arc; with centre B and radius 6 cm, draw an arc meeting it at C. Join AC and BC; thus CA = 5.2 cm and BC = 6 cm.

For each vertex A, B and C, mark points 1 cm from the vertex on both arms of its angle. With these two points as centres and radius 1.5 cm, draw arcs intersecting inside the angle; join the vertex to the intersection to construct its angle bisector.
The bisectors AI and BI meet at I. Draw CI and verify that it passes through I.
Thus, the three angle bisectors are concurrent at I.

written.text: Define circumcentre of the triangle.

written.text: Prove that any point equidistant from the end points of a line segment is on the right bisector of it. OR Prove that parallelograms on equal bases and having the same (or equal) altitude are equal in area.
modelAnswer: First proof: Let M be the midpoint of AB and join P to M.
PA=PB (given), AM=BM (M is the midpoint), and PM=PM (common side).
Since these angles form a linear pair, each is 90°; hence PM⊥AB and P lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
OR: Let the equal bases of the parallelograms be b and their equal altitudes be h.
Therefore, the parallelograms have equal areas.

written.text: Prove that “Any point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from its arms.” OR Prove that “Triangles on the same base and of same altitude are equal in area”
modelAnswer: OR — Any point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from its arms:
Let OP bisect ∠AOB. Draw PM ⟂ OA and PN ⟂ OB.
In right triangles OMP and ONP, OP is the common hypotenuse.
Hence PM = PN, so P is equidistant from the arms of the angle.
OR — Triangles on the same base and of the same altitude are equal in area:
Let the common base be b and the common altitude be h.
Therefore, the two triangles have equal areas.

rubric.description: States the triangle inequality and applies it to explain impossibility.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that \(3+4\) must be greater than 7, not equal to it.

written.text: Construct a triangle XYZ: m∠Z = 6.4cm, m∠Y = 2.4cm, m∠Y = 90°
modelAnswer: Interpreting the given lengths as \(XZ=6.4\) cm and \(XY=2.4\) cm, with \(∠ Y=90^°\):
At Y, construct a ray perpendicular to XY, so \(∠ XYZ=90^°\).
With centre X and radius 6.4 cm, draw an arc cutting the perpendicular ray at Z; thus \(XZ=6.4\) cm.
Join XZ. Triangle XYZ is the required triangle.
written.followUp: Construct triangle ABC with \(AC=5.0\) cm, \(AB=3.0\) cm and \(∠ B=90^°\).

rubric.why: This uses the given 2.4 cm side as the base of the right-angle construction.

rubric.why: The remaining side and right angle determine the required triangle.
rubric.description: Locates Z using the 6.4 cm side and completes the triangle.
rubric.how: Award for marking Z at 6.4 cm from X on the perpendicular ray and joining XZ.

written.text: Construct the △ABC and draw perpendicular bisectors of its sides: mBC = 2.9cm, m∠B = 60°, m∠A = 30°
modelAnswer: At B, construct a ray making ∠ABC = 60° with BC.
At C, construct a ray perpendicular to BC; let it meet the ray from B at A.
The resulting triangle has AB = 5.8 cm and AC = 2.9√3 cm (approximately 5.02 cm).
For BC, with compass radius 2 cm (> 1.45 cm), draw arcs from B and C above and below BC; join the arc intersections to obtain its perpendicular bisector.
For AB and AC, use compass radius 3 cm (> half of either side); draw arcs from the endpoints of each side and join the two arc intersections to obtain each perpendicular bisector.
Label the three perpendicular bisectors of AB, BC and AC.
written.followUp: Construct a triangle PQR with QR = 4 cm, ∠Q = 45° and ∠P = 30°, then draw the perpendicular bisectors of its sides.

rubric.why: The construction starts with the given side and the given angle at B.
rubric.description: Draws BC and constructs the 60° ray at B.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing BC = 2.9 cm and a ray making ∠ABC = 60°.

rubric.why: The angle sum gives ∠C = 90°, which determines the ray from C and locates A.
rubric.description: Constructs the third vertex using the angle sum of a triangle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for finding ∠C = 90°, drawing the perpendicular at C and marking its intersection with the ray from B as A.

rubric.why: The perpendicular bisectors are constructed with arcs from the endpoints of each side; the chosen radii exceed half the corresponding side lengths.
rubric.description: Shows suitable compass-arc construction for the perpendicular bisectors.

written.text: Construct triangle ABC in which: mAB = 2.5cm, m∠A = 30°, m∠B = 105°
modelAnswer: Draw AB = 2.5 cm using a ruler.
At A, construct a ray making an angle of 30° with AB.
At B, on the same side of AB, construct a ray making an angle of 105° with BA.
Mark the intersection of the two rays as C. Triangle ABC is the required triangle.

rubric.how: At A construct a 30° ray; at B construct a 105° ray on the same side of AB. Label their intersection C.

written.text: Construct triangle PQR and draw its altitudes: mRP = 3.6cm, m∠Q = 30°, m∠P = 105°
modelAnswer: At P, construct a ray such that ∠QPR = 105°.
At R, construct a ray such that ∠PRQ = 180° − 105° − 30° = 45°; the rays meet at Q.
Draw the perpendicular from P to line QR, the perpendicular from Q to line PR, and the perpendicular from R to line PQ; these are the three altitudes.

perpendicular from Q to line PR
perpendicular from R to line PQ

written.text: Construct ΔXYZ, in which m ZX = 6.4 cm, m YZ = 2.4 cm, and m ∠Y = 90°.

written.text: Construct a ΔABC, m AB = 3.2 cm, m BC = 4.2 cm, m CA = 5.2 cm

written.text: Construct ΔABC in which: m AB = 2.5 cm, m∠A = 30°, m∠B = 105°.

modelAnswer: At B, construct a 60° ray to BC; at C, construct a 90° ray to CB.

written.text: Construct a ΔABC in which: m AB = 2.5 cm, m∠A = 30°, m∠B = 105°.
modelAnswer: At A, construct a ray making ∠BAC = 30° with AB.

written.text: Construct the ΔABC. Draw the perpendicular bisectors of its sides: m AB = 5.3 cm, m∠A = 45°, m∠B = 30°.
modelAnswer: At A, construct a ray making 45° with AB; at B, construct a ray making 30° with BA on the same side of AB.
Let the rays intersect at C. Then ΔABC is constructed; ∠C = 180° − 45° − 30° = 105°.

written.text:
Any point on the right bisector of a line segment is equidistant from its end points.
OR
Any point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from its arms.
modelAnswer: Let P lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB, meeting AB at M.
Then AM = BM and PM ⟂ AB, so ∠AMP = ∠BMP = 90°; also PM is common.
Hence PA = PB, so P is equidistant from A and B.
Let P lie on the bisector of ∠AOB. Draw PM ⟂ OA and PN ⟂ OB.
Thus ΔOMP ≅ ΔONP by hypotenuse–acute angle (HA).
Hence PM = PN, so P is equidistant from the arms of the angle.
written.followUp: Prove that any point on the perpendicular bisector of a line segment is equidistant from its endpoints.

rubric.why: A proof needs the equal lengths and common side for the perpendicular-bisector case, or the common hypotenuse and equal angles for the angle-bisector case.
rubric.description: Sets up the relevant pair of triangles and identifies their equal parts.
rubric.how: Award for a valid setup in either proof option.

rubric.why: The perpendicular condition gives right angles in the relevant triangles.
rubric.description: Identifies the right angles in the triangle comparison.
rubric.how: Award for explicitly using the right angles in the chosen proof.

rubric.why: Congruence establishes equality of the corresponding distances.
rubric.description: Proves the relevant triangles congruent using a valid criterion.
rubric.how: Award for SAS in the perpendicular-bisector proof or hypotenuse–acute angle (HA) in the angle-bisector proof.

rubric.why: The conclusion is that the point has equal distances to the endpoints or to the two arms, as appropriate.
rubric.how: Award for the conclusion in either proof option.

written.text: Construct ΔXYZ m∠Y = 90°, m∠Z = 6.4cm, mYZ = 2.4cm

Draw a ray from Y and mark Z on it so that YZ = 2.4 cm.

written.text: Construct the triangle ABC and draw the perpendicular bisectors of its sides. mAB = 5.3cm, m∠A = 45°, m∠B = 30°
modelAnswer: At A construct a 45° ray above AB; at B construct a 30° ray above BA.
Name the intersection of the two rays C, and join AC and BC to construct ΔABC.
Set the compass opening to 3 cm. For side AB, draw equal arcs from A and B above and below the side, then join the two arc intersections to make its perpendicular bisector.
Using the same 3 cm compass opening, repeat the arc construction from A and C, then join the arc intersections to bisect AC perpendicularly.
Repeat from B and C, then join the arc intersections to bisect BC perpendicularly.
The three constructed lines are the perpendicular bisectors of AB, AC and BC.

modelAnswer: An altitude (or height) of a triangle is the perpendicular line segment drawn from a vertex to the opposite side or to the line containing the opposite side.

modelAnswer: At B, construct a 60° ray to BC.

written.text: Prove that any point on the right bisector of a line segment is equidistant from its end points. OR Prove that the triangles on the same base and of the same (i.e. equal) altitudes are equal in area.
modelAnswer: Proof 1: Let AB be a line segment, CD its perpendicular bisector, and P any point on CD.
Let CD intersect AB at O. Since CD bisects AB, OA = OB.
OP = OP, since OP is common to △AOP and △BOP.
Hence AP = BP, as corresponding sides of congruent triangles.
Proof 2: Let the two triangles have the same base b and equal altitudes h.
Let their areas be A1 and A2.
Therefore A1 = A2, so the two triangles are equal in area.

rubric.how: Award for OA = OB in the first proof, or for both the same-base and equal-altitude facts in the area proof.

rubric.why: The first proof identifies the common side and equal right angles; the alternative applies the triangle area formula to both triangles.

written.text: Prove that the right bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent. OR Prove that parallelograms on equal bases and having the same (or equal) altitude are equal in area.
modelAnswer: Option 1: Perpendicular bisectors of the sides are concurrent.
Let the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC meet at O.
Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, OA = OB.
Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC, OB = OC.
Hence O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC as well.
Thus, the three perpendicular bisectors pass through O and are concurrent.
Option 2: Parallelograms on equal bases and with equal altitudes have equal areas.
Let the two parallelograms have equal bases b and equal altitudes h.
Area of the first parallelogram = b × h.
Area of the second parallelogram = b × h.
Therefore, the two parallelograms have equal areas.

rubric.why: These facts complete either proof by establishing concurrence or equality of areas.

written.text: Any point inside an angle equidistant from its arms is on the bisector of it. Prove it. OR Triangles on equal bases and of equal altitudes are equal in area. Prove it.
modelAnswer: Let AX be the angle, and let X be a point inside it; draw XM ⟂ one arm and XN ⟂ the other arm.
Since X is equidistant from the arms, XM = XN.
In right triangles △AMX and △ANX, AX is common and XM = XN; therefore △AMX ≅ △ANX by RHS.

written.text: Any point on the right bisector of a line segment is equidistant from its end points. Prove it. OR Prove that triangles on equal base and of equal altitudes are equal in area.
modelAnswer: Alternative 1: Let AB be the segment, M its midpoint, and P any point on its perpendicular bisector.
Since M is the midpoint, MA = MB.
Because PM is perpendicular to AB, ∠PMA = ∠PMB = 90°.
PM = PM (common side), so △PMA ≅ △PMB by SAS.
Therefore PA = PB, and P is equidistant from A and B.
Alternative 2: Let two triangles have equal bases and equal corresponding altitudes, with base length b and altitude h.
The area of each triangle = 1/2 bh.
Since the bases and altitudes are equal, the areas are equal.

Since AM = BM, PA = PB, and PM = PM (common), △PAM ≅ △PBM by SSS.

Area of each triangle = 1/2 × b × h.
Therefore, the two triangles have equal areas.

written.text: Prove that any point on the right bisector of a line segment is equidistant from its end points. OR Prove that triangles on the same base and of the same (equal) altitudes are equal in area.
modelAnswer: Proof 1 (right bisector): Let AB be the line segment, M its midpoint, and P any point on its perpendicular bisector.
Since M is the midpoint, AM = BM.
Since PM is perpendicular to AB, ∠PMA = ∠PMB = 90°.
Hence, PA = PB; therefore P is equidistant from the endpoints A and B.
Proof 2 (equal areas): Let the two triangles have the same base b and equal altitudes h.
Area of the first triangle = 1/2 bh.
Area of the second triangle = 1/2 bh.
Therefore, the two triangles have equal areas.

modelAnswer: To prove that the bisectors of the angles of a triangle are concurrent:
Let the bisectors of ∠A and ∠B intersect at I.
Since I lies on the bisector of ∠A, d(I,AB)=d(I,AC).
Since I lies on the bisector of ∠B, d(I,AB)=d(I,BC).
Therefore, d(I,AC)=d(I,BC), so I lies on bisector ∠C.
Hence all three angle bisectors are concurrent.
To prove that triangles on equal bases and of equal altitudes are equal in area:
Let b1 and b2 be the base lengths, and h1 and h2 the corresponding altitudes.
Area of the first triangle, A1=1/2 b1h1.
Area of the second triangle, A2=1/2 b2h2.
Therefore, A1=A2, so the triangles are equal in area.

Measure and mark the midpoint N of ZX: ZN = NX = 2.8 cm.
Measure and mark the midpoint P of XY: XP = PY = 2.25 cm.
Join X to M, Y to N and Z to P. These are the three medians.

(b) Let the bisectors of ∠A and ∠B of △ABC meet at I.
Since I lies on the bisector of ∠A, its perpendicular distances from AB and AC are equal.
Since I lies on the bisector of ∠B, its perpendicular distances from AB and BC are equal.

(a) Solve the Equation. x/(3x − 6) = 2 − 2x/(x − 2), x ≠ 2
(b) Prove that: (Cotθ + Cosecθ)(tanθ − Sinθ) = Secθ − Cosθ.
modelAnswer: Thus, x/[3(x − 2)] = −4/(x − 2). Since x ≠ 2, multiply by 3(x − 2): x = −12.
(b) L.H.S. = (Cos θ/Sin θ + 1/Sin θ)(Sin θ/Cos θ − Sin θ).
= ((1 + Cos θ)/Sin θ)(Sin θ(1 − Cos θ)/Cos θ).
= (1 − Cos² θ)/Cos θ = Sin² θ/Cos θ.
= 1/Cos θ − Cos θ = Sec θ − Cos θ = R.H.S.
